ranges.Grallaria rufula: Andes of Venezuela (Táchira) and eastern Andes of Colombia southward to Cundinamarca and western Meta (but absent from the west slope in the Iguaque Massif in Boyacá and far southwestern Santander)
ranges.Grallaria rufocinerea: central Andes of Colombia (from Antioquia southward) to eastern Andes of far northern Ecuador (northwestern Sucumbíos)
ranges.Grallaria alvarezi: western Andes of Colombia (northwestern Antioquia southward to northwestern Cauca)
ranges.Grallaria saturata: central Andes of Colombia southward through Ecuador to northern Peru (north and west of the Río Marañón); also on the west slope of the eastern Andes of Colombia, in the Iguaque Massif in Boyacá, and far southwestern Santander
ranges.Grallaria blakei: east slope of the Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas south of the Río Marañón, southward to Huánuco, and north of the Río Huallaga)
ranges.Grallaria gravesi: east slope of the Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas south of the Río Marañón, southward to Huánuco, and north of the Río Huallaga)
ranges.Grallaria oneilli: east slope of the Andes of central Peru (Huánuco south of the Río Huallaga and Pasco north of the Río Perené)
ranges.Grallaria obscura: east slope of the Andes of central Peru (Junín, south of the Río Perené and Río Paucartambo, north of the Río Mantaro, and west of the Río Ene)
ranges.Grallaria centralis: east slope of the Andes of central Peru (Huánuco south of the Río Huallaga southward through Pasco to Junín, west of the Río Ene, and north of the Río Mantaro)
ranges.Grallaria ayacuchensis: east slope of the Andes of south-central Peru (Ayacucho, west of the Río Apurímac between the Río Mantaro and Río Pampas)
ranges.Grallaria occabambae: humid montane forest and scrub and bamboo stands in the Andes of southeastern Peru, from Junin southward to Cusco
ranges.Grallaria cochabambae: east slope of the Andes of northwestern Bolivia (La Paz, Cochabamba, and adjacent Santa Cruz)
ranges.Grallaria sinaensis: east slope of the Andes of far southeastern Peru (Puno) and adjacent Bolivia (far western La Paz)
ranges.Grallaria dignissima: far southeastern Colombia (western Putumayo) to eastern Ecuador and northeastern Peru
ranges.Grallaria eludens: lowlands of eastern Peru (Ucayali and Madre de Dios) and adjacent Brazil (Acre)
ranges.Grallaria ridgelyi: Andes of southern Ecuador (upper Río Chinchipe drainage)
ranges.Grallaria carrikeri: east slope of Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas and La Libertad)
ranges.Grallaria nuchalis: humid montane forest and bamboo stands in the western and central Andes of Colombia, also locally in the western slope of the eastern Andes in northern Colombia, southward to northwestern Ecuador, and from southeastern Colombia southward to far northern Peru
ranges.Grallaria albigula: Andes of southeastern Peru and western Bolivia to far northwestern Argentina
ranges.Grallaria watkinsi: lowlands and Andes of southwestern Ecuador and northwestern Peru (Tumbes)
ranges.Grallaria ruficapilla: humid montane cloudforest, humid to semi-humid scrub and woodland, bamboo stands in the coastal mountains of north-central Venezuela, in the Sierra de Perijá, and the Andes from western Venezuela southward to northern Peru
ranges.Grallaria flavotincta: west slope of western Andes of Colombia and northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Grallaria urraoensis: northern part of western Andes of Colombia (Antioquia)
ranges.Grallaria milleri: humid montane cloudforest in the central Andes of Colombia (western slope of the Central Andes in Caldas, Risaralda, and Quindio, and on the eastern slope in Tolima)
ranges.Grallaria bangsi: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (northeastern Colombia)
ranges.Grallaria kaestneri: eastern Andes of Colombia (Cundinamarca and Meta)
ranges.Grallaria quitensis: central Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, and far northern Peru
ranges.Grallaria atuensis: Andes of northern Peru (southern Amazonas and eastern La Libertad)
ranges.Grallaria hypoleuca: montane cloudforest and bamboo stands in the central and eastern Andes of Colombia, southward along the eastern Andes of Ecuador to far northern Peru
ranges.Grallaria erythroleuca: Andes of southeastern Peru in Cusco (Vilcabamba and Vilcanota Mountains)
ranges.Grallaria erythrotis: Yungas of western Bolivia (La Paz, Cochabamba, and Santa Cruz)
ranges.Grallaria przewalskii: east slope of Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas to eastern La Libertad)
ranges.Grallaria capitalis: east slope of Andes of Peru (Junín, Pasco, and Huánuco)
ranges.Scelorchilus albicollis: xeric scrub from north-central to south-central Chile (southwestern Antofagasta southward to Maule)
ranges.Scelorchilus rubecula: humid coniferous and Nothofagus forests with dense shrubby patches; also deciduous forest and woodland from south-central Chile (including Mocha Island) to southern Chile (from Bío Bío southward to Aisén) and adjacent southwestern Argentina and immediately adjacent parts of Argentina (Neuquén southward to western Chubut)
ranges.Pteroptochos megapodius: slopes with scattered bushes and scrub, semiarid rocky outcrops, and boulders from north-central to south-central Chile (Atacama to Bío Bío)
ranges.Pteroptochos tarnii: southern Chile, from Río Biobío (also locally on right bank south of Río Laja) southward to northern Magallanes, and adjacent western Argentina (from western Neuquén southward to southwestern Santa Cruz); could occur locally farther south
ranges.Pteroptochos castaneus: central Chile (Colchagua to Río Biobío) and adjacent northwestern Neuquén (west-central Argentina)
ranges.Psilorhamphus guttatus: southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais) to northeastern Argentina and (?) southeastern Paraguay
ranges.Liosceles thoracicus: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from southern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia and eastward in Brazil, south of the Amazon River, to the Rio Tapajos in western Pará
ranges.Acropternis orthonyx: humid montane forest and bamboo stands in the Andes from western Venezuela southward to far northern Peru (southern Amazonas); in the western Andes only in northwestern Colombia and again in northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Teledromas fuscus: Andean slope of Argentina (southwestern Salta to Río Negro)
ranges.Rhinocrypta lanceolata: thorn forest and scrub in the Chaco region and slopes of the Andes from southeastern Bolivia and western Paraguay southward to central Argentina (northern Río Negro)
ranges.Merulaxis ater: southeastern Brazil (southern Bahia and Espírito Santo to eastern Paraná and Santa Catarina)
ranges.Merulaxis stresemanni: coastal eastern Brazil (Bahia); rare and local
ranges.Eleoscytalopus indigoticus: southeastern Brazil (eastern Bahia to Santa Catarina and northeastern Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Eleoscytalopus psychopompus: coastal lowlands of eastern Brazil (southeastern Bahia)
ranges.Myornis senilis: Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, and northern Peru (south to Pasco)
ranges.Eugralla paradoxa: south-central Chile (Santiago to Chiloé) and adjacent Argentina; Mocha Island
ranges.Scytalopus iraiensis: southwestern Brazil (river basins in Iguaçu and Tibagi, eastern Paraná)
ranges.Scytalopus speluncae: southeastern Brazil (southwestern Espírito Santo to northern Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Scytalopus novacapitalis: southern Brazil (southern Goiás, Distrito Federal, and western Minas Gerais)
ranges.Scytalopus diamantinensis: Chapada Diamantina region of northeastern Brazil (Bahia)
ranges.Scytalopus pachecoi: northeastern Argentina (Misiones) and far southern Brazil (southwestern Paraná to southern Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Scytalopus petrophilus: central and southern Minas Gerais, Brazil
ranges.Scytalopus magellanicus: Andes of central Chile and Argentina to Tierra del Fuego
ranges.Scytalopus fuscus: Andes of central Chile (Atacama to Biobío)
ranges.Scytalopus affinis: western Andes of Peru (southern Cajamarca to Ancash)
ranges.Scytalopus krabbei: east slope of the Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas, south of the Río Marañón, to Huánuco, north of the Río Huallaga)
ranges.Scytalopus opacus: central Andes of Colombia to east-central Ecuador
ranges.Scytalopus androstictus: Andes of southeastern Ecuador and far northern Peru
ranges.Scytalopus superciliaris: undergrowth of Polylepis and alder woodland in the Andes of northwestern Argentina from Jujuy southward to La Rioja
ranges.Scytalopus simonsi: Andes of southeastern Peru (Vilcanota Mountains) to central Bolivia (Cochabamba)
ranges.Scytalopus zimmeri: Andes of southern Bolivia (Chuquisaca and Tarija) and northwestern Argentina (Jujuy and Salta)
ranges.Scytalopus schulenbergi: Andes of southeastern Peru (Vilcanota Mountains) to central Bolivia (Cochabamba)
ranges.Scytalopus urubambae: Andes of east-central Peru (southern Cordillera Vilcabamba)
ranges.Scytalopus whitneyi: Andes of south-central Peru (Ayacucho and Apurímac)
ranges.Scytalopus altirostris: central Andes of Peru (southern Amazonas to Huánuco)
ranges.Scytalopus frankeae: Andes of central Peru (Pasco and Junín)
ranges.Scytalopus parvirostris: Andes of northwestern Peru to east-central Bolivia (Santa Cruz)
ranges.Scytalopus bolivianus: Andes of southeastern Peru (Ayacucho and Puno) to southern Bolivia (Chuquisaca)
ranges.Scytalopus sanctaemartae: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (northeastern Colombia)
ranges.Scytalopus atratus: undergrowth of humid foothill and montane forest in the Sierra de Perijá and the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the Andes of Colombia and eastern Andes of Ecuador to far northern Peru north of the Río Marañón; also in the eastern Andes of Peru south and east of the Río Marañón, southward to southeastern Peru, in Puno, including Cerros del Sira
ranges.Scytalopus vicinior: Pacific slope of southwestern Colombia (Risaralda) to Ecuador (Cotopaxi)
ranges.Scytalopus argentifrons: montane forest from northwestern Costa Rica to central Panama
ranges.Scytalopus panamensis: eastern Panama and adjacent northern Colombia (Cerro Tacarcuna massif)
ranges.Scytalopus chocoensis: Pacific slope of eastern Panama (Cerro Pirre) to northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Scytalopus rodriguezi: undergrowth of humid montane forest in Serrania de los Yariguies and in the eastern slope and the headwaters of the Magdalena Valley in the central Andes of Colombia
ranges.Scytalopus robbinsi: Pacific slope of southwestern Ecuador (Azuay and El Oro)
ranges.Scytalopus alvarezlopezi: Pacific slope of Colombian Andes (western Antioquia southward to southwestern Valle del Cauca)
ranges.Scytalopus caracae: coastal mountains of northern Venezuela (Aragua to Miranda)
ranges.Scytalopus meridanus: montane humid forest and edge of Andes of western to north-central Venezuela
ranges.Scytalopus latebricola: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (northeastern Colombia)
ranges.Scytalopus spillmanni: central Andes of Colombia to central Ecuador
ranges.Scytalopus parkeri: Andes of southern Ecuador to far northern Peru (eastern Piura and northern Cajamarca)
ranges.Scytalopus griseicollis: undergrowth of humid montane forest, bamboo stands, and elfin forest in the Andes of western Venezuela and northeastern Colombia, including Serrania de los Yariguies, southward to southern Cundinamarca
ranges.Scytalopus femoralis: east slope of Andes of eastern Peru (Amazonas to Junín)
ranges.Scytalopus micropterus: Andes of Colombia to Ecuador and far northern Peru
ranges.Scytalopus latrans: undergrowth of humid montane forest and humid to semi-humid montane scrub in the Andes from western Venezuela (Táchira and Mérida) southward to northern Peru (in Piura, Cajamarca, and Lambayeque), north and south of the Río Marañón
ranges.Scytalopus acutirostris: central Andes of Peru (eastern La Libertad to Junín)
ranges.Scytalopus unicolor: Andes of northern Peru (southern Cajamarca and La Libertad) and adjacent Ecuador
ranges.Scytalopus intermedius: central Andes of northern Peru (southern Amazonas)
ranges.Scytalopus macropus: east slope of central Andes of Peru (southern Amazonas to Junín)
ranges.Chamaeza nobilis: tropical rainforest in the western Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia, and in Brazil eastward to central Pará, south of the Amazon River
ranges.Chamaeza campanisona: humid montane and lowland forest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela and the tepuis of southern Venezuela and adjacent Brazil and Guyana; in the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the eastern Andes to south-central Bolivia; also in the Atlantic Forest region from northeastern Brazil, in southern Bahia, southward to central Rio Grande do Sul, far northeastern Argentina and eastern Paraguay, and isolated in northeastern Brazil in Alagoas and Ceará
ranges.Chamaeza ruficauda: southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais to northern Rio Grande do Sul) and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Chamaeza meruloides: southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo to northeastern Santa Catarina)
ranges.Chamaeza mollissima: montane cloudforest in locally in the western and central Andes of Colombia, and the eastern Andes from northeastern Colombia southward to northern Peru north of the Río Marañón, and patchily along the eastern Andes of Peru southward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Chamaeza turdina: humid montane forest in the coastal mountains of north-central Venezuela and patchily in the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia southward to the headwaters of the Río Magdalena (Huila)
ranges.Formicarius rufifrons: southeastern Peru (Madre de Dios), adjacent western Brazil, and northwestern Bolivia
ranges.Formicarius colma: tropical rainforest and gallery forest in savannas in the Guiana Shield, Orinoco and Amazon basins from eastern Venezuela and the Guianas southward across the entire Amazon basin to northern Bolivia; also in the Atlantic Forest from northeastern Brazil, in Paraiba, southward to northernmost Rio Grande do Sul
ranges.Formicarius rufipectus: humid montane cloudforest in the mountains of Costa Rica, western and eastern Panama, and adjacent Colombia; also locally in Sierra de Perijá and the Andes of westernmost Venezuela and along the central and western Andes of Colombia southward across Ecuador to far northern Peru north of the Río Marañón; in the eastern Andes of Peru south of the Río Marañón southward to southeastern Peru (Cusco)
ranges.Formicarius moniliger: humid lowland forest on Caribbean slope of southern Veracruz and northern Oaxaca eastward through Yucatan Peninsula (excluding Cozumel), eastward through north-central Honduras
ranges.Formicarius analis: tropical humid forest in the Caribbean slope of eastern Honduras southward to Panama and in the Pacific slope of Costa Rica and Panama; in northern Colombia and western Venezuela; east of the Andes in the foothills of the Andes of western Venezuela and northeastern Colombia, in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, Trinidad, eastern Venezuela and the Guianas southward across central and eastern Amazon basin in Brazil, and in the western Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to central Bolivia
ranges.Formicarius nigricapillus: Caribbean slope of northwestern to central Costa Rica and both slopes of Panama
ranges.Formicarius destructus: tropical Pacific Colombia and western Ecuador
ranges.Sclerurus mexicanus: humid forest of foothills and mountains on Caribbean slope from Hidalgo (east-central Mexico) through northern Oaxaca to southern Belize and through eastern Panama
ranges.Sclerurus rufigularis: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from central and southern Venezuela and the Guianas southward across the Brazilian Amazon to northeastern Bolivia, and in the western Amazon of Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia
ranges.Sclerurus obscurior: tropical rainforest to montane cloudforest in the lowlands and Andean foothills from eastern Panama and western Venezuela southward along the western Andes of Colombia to Valle del Cauca, central Andes to Tolima and eastern Andes to Putumayo; west of the Andes in the Pacific lowlands of western Colombia southward to southwestern Ecuador; east of the Andes locally in eastern and southern Venezuela and the Guianas southward to the eastern Amazon of Brazil southward to Tocantins and eastward to northern Maranhão, and westward to the western Amazon in southeastern Colombia, eastern Ecuador and Peru to northern Bolivia; also in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil from central Bahia (possible further north from Alagoas) southward to Paraná
ranges.Sclerurus guatemalensis: humid lowland to hill forest of Caribbean slope from southeastern Veracruz and northern Oaxaca eastward through southern Yucatan Peninsula to northern Nicaragua, thence both slopes from southeastern Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica through north-central Colombia, west of the Andes to northwestern Colombia and (perhaps disjunctly) northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Sclerurus caudacutus: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from central and eastern Venezuela and the Guianas south across the Brazilian Amazon to eastern Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and northwestern Bolivia; in Brazil eastward to eastern Maranhão and southward to northern Mato Grosso; also in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil in Pernambuco southward to Espirito Santo
ranges.Sclerurus scansor: humid forest from northeastern Brazil in Ceará southward across interior Brazil to Goiás, Minas Gerais, and central Bahia, and in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil from southern Bahia southward to Rio Grande do Sul and westward to eastern Paraguay and northern Argentina in Misiones
ranges.Sclerurus albigularis: humid forest in montane areas from northwestern Costa Rica to western Panama; in South America from Trinidad and Tobago westward to the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela from Monagas west to western Lara, and in the Andes from western Venezuela, Sierra de Perijá, and Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta southward along the eastern slope of the eastern Andes of Colombia to southeastern Peru; in southeastern Amazonia of Peru extends eastward to the lowlands to Acre, Rondônia and Mato Grosso, in Brazil, and southward to northwestern Bolivia
ranges.Geositta peruviana: arid littoral of far northern coastal Peru from northern Tumbes to Ica (south-central coast)
ranges.Geositta tenuirostris: dry paramo and puna in central Ecuador and from northern Peru, west and south of the Río Marañón, southward across Peru and Bolivia to northern and western Argentina southward to Mendoza
ranges.Geositta punensis: Andes of far southern Peru to western Bolivia, northern Chile, and northwestern Argentina
ranges.Geositta cunicularia: grassland and arid scrub from the Andes of central Peru, in Huánuco, southeastward to western Bolivia, northern Chile, and northwestern Argentina, and in southeastern Brazil from Santa Catarina southward across Uruguay to eastern Buenos Aires, Argentina; migrates southward across Argentina to Tierra del Fuego; also in the coast of southern Peru from Ica southward to southern Chile
ranges.Geositta poeciloptera: south-central Brazil (Minas Gerais to São Paulo) and adjacent northeastern Bolivia
ranges.Geositta crassirostris: west slope of Andes of Peru (Lima southward to Arequipa)
ranges.Geositta rufipennis: grassland and arid scrub in the Andes of western Bolivia from southeastern La Paz southward to southern Chile and southern Argentina in Santa Cruz
ranges.Geositta maritima: arid littoral of Peru (Ancash) to northern Chile (Atacama)
ranges.Geositta saxicolina: Andes of central Peru (western Junín, Huancavelica, Lima, and Pasco)
ranges.Geositta isabellina: Andes of central Chile and adjacent western Argentina
ranges.Geositta antarctica: breeds southern Chile and southern Argentina; winters northward to Mendoza
ranges.Glyphorynchus spirurus: humid forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in eastern Mexico (from northern Oaxaca and southern Veracruz) southeastward to eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia, and in the Pacific lowlands of southern Costa Rica and western Panama; in northern Colombia and western Venezuela, southward along the Magdalena Valley to Cundinamarca, and west of the Andes southward to southwestern Ecuador; east of the Andes in the eastern foothills of the Andes of southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia, and in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from northeastern Venezuela and the Guianas southward across the entire Amazon of Brazil, eastern Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, southward to central Bolivia; in Brazil eastward to northern Maranhão, southward to central Mato Grosso; also in the Atlantic Forest from northern Bahia southward to Espirito Santo
ranges.Certhiasomus stictolaemus: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from eastern Colombia southward to eastern Peru in Ucayali and eastward to southern Venezuela and most of the Brazilian Amazon northeastward to Amapá and eastern French Guiana, eastward to northern Maranhão and southward to eastern Rondônia and northern Mato Grosso; also isolated in central Guyana and Suriname
ranges.Sittasomus griseicapillus: deciduous to humid forest from northern Mexico in the Gulf of Mexico slope from southern Nuevo León and Tamaulipas southeastward across Central America, including the Yucatan Peninsula, to southern Nicaragua, and on the Pacific slope from Nayarit to eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia; in the lowlands of northern Colombia and western Venezuela southward in interior Colombia along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys (to Quindio and Cundinamarca); west of the Andes in far southwestern Colombia southward to far northern Peru; in the foothills of the Andes and coastal mountains of western and northern Venezuela eastward to the Paría Peninsula and Tobago, and in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from central and southern Venezuela, Guyana, and French Guiana westward and southward across Amazonian Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, and eastward across interior Brazil to the Atlantic Forest southward to northernmost Uruguay and northeastern Argentina southward to Santa Fe, and in the Yungas of Bolivia southward to Argentina southward to Catamarca and La Rioja
ranges.Deconychura longicauda: the Guianas and Brazil north of the Amazon River (from Rio Negro eastward to Amapá)
ranges.Deconychura typica: mostly humid forest from eastern Honduras and northern Nicaragua and from western Costa Rica and adjacent Nicaragua eastward to northern and eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia, in northern Colombia near the Andes (northward to Córdoba and Bolívar), southward to the lower Magdalena Valley (northern Tolima)
ranges.Deconychura pallida: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from southern Venezuela southward across southeastern Colombia and eastern Ecuador (mostly in the foothills of the Andes) southward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz), and in Brazil eastward to eastern Pará and adjacent Maranhão, and southward to northern Mato Grosso and Rondônia
ranges.Dendrocincla tyrannina: montane cloudforest in the Andes from far southwestern Venezuela southward along the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia to northern Peru north of the Río Marañón (Cajamarca), and from northern Peru south of the Marañón, southward in the eastern Andes to far northwestern Bolivia
ranges.Dendrocincla merula: tropical rainforest in the Río Orinoco and Amazon basins from central and eastern Venezuela and the Guianas, southwestward to eastern Colombia and northeastern Ecuador southward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz); in Brazil across the entire Amazon eastward to northeastern Maranhão, southward to western Mato Grosso and Rondônia
ranges.Dendrocincla homochroa: humid to deciduous forest and woodland in the Gulf of Mexico slope from northern Oaxaca (Mexico) southeastward across Central America, including the Yucatan Peninsula, to eastern Panama, and in the Pacific slope from southern Oaxaca to western El Salvador; in South America in far northwestern Colombia and in the foothills of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá and the Andes of western Venezuela and northeastern Colombia
ranges.Dendrocincla turdina: humid and gallery forest in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil, from Pernambuco and Alagoas southward to northern Rio Grande do Sul and westward to Paraná, northeastern Argentina (Misiones), and eastern Paraguay
ranges.Dendrocincla anabatina: humid forest (mainly) of lowlands to hills on Caribbean slope from southern Veracruz and eastern Oaxaca through Yucatan Peninsula (but not Cozumel) through far north-central Costa Rica, then disjunctly in west-central Costal Rica to adjacent far southwestern Panama
ranges.Dendrocincla fuliginosa: mostly humid forest from eastern Honduras southward along the Caribbean slope of Nicaragua and Costa Rica to eastern Panama; in northern Colombia and northern Venezuela eastward to Trinidad and Tobago, the Guianas and northeastern Brazil; in central Colombia southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys (to Quindio and Cundinamarca), and west of the Andes southward across western Colombia to northwesternmost Peru; in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from southern Venezuela southward across the Amazon of Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, southward to central Bolivia Brazil (eastward to northern Maranhão and western Tocantins, and southward to southern Mato Grosso)
ranges.Nasica longirostris: eastern Colombia to southwestern Venezuela, northern Bolivia, Amazonian Brazil, and French Guiana
ranges.Dendrexetastes rufigula: tropical rainforest, gallery and savanna forest, riparian woodland and river islands in the Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to northern Bolivia (southward to northern Cochabamba and western Santa Cruz), and eastward across the Amazon of Brazil to northeastern Brazil, in Amapá, eastern Pará and adjacent Maranhão, and northward to the Guianas and far eastern Venezuela, in the lower Río Orinoco basin
ranges.Dendrocolaptes sanctithomae: humid forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in eastern Mexico (from northern Oaxaca and adjacent Veracruz) and in the Pacific slope from eastern Guerrero southeastward across Central America to northern Colombia and western Venezuela, southward along the Magdalena Valley to Cundinamarca; west of the Andes southward along western Colombia to northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Dendrocolaptes certhia: tropical rainforest and semi-deciduous and gallery forest and woodland in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from eastern Venezuela and the Guianas southwestward to the western Amazon in eastern Colombi southward to central Bolivia; across Amazonian Brazil (to northern Maranhão and western Tocantins, and southward to Mato Grosso); disjunctly in far northeastern Brazil (Alagoas and Pernambuco)
ranges.Dendrocolaptes platyrostris: humid forest in the Atlantic Forest region to semi-deciduous and gallery woodland in the Cerrado, Caatinga, and Chaco from northeastern Brazil (northern Maranhão, Piauí and Ceará) southward across eastern and interior Brazil to Rio Grande do Sul and adjacent Uruguay, southern Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, easterm Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina (southward to Chaco and northern Corrientes)
ranges.Dendrocolaptes hoffmannsi: southern Amazonian Brazil south of the Amazon River to Rondônia and southern Mato Grosso
ranges.Dendrocolaptes picumnus: deciduous to humid forest, and pine and pine-oak forest in eastern Mexico (Chiapas), southeastward across mountains of Guatemala to northern Nicaragua, and in Costa Rica and western Panama; in foothills and slopes of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, and the Andes of western Venezuela and Colombia; east of the Andes in the Río Orinoco and Amazon basins from central Venezuela southward across the Amazon of Brazil (eastward to eastern Pará and southward to Mato Grosso) to eastern Colombia and Ecuador southward to central Bolivia, southward along the Yungas to northwestern Argentina, and southward across the Chaco of eastern Bolivia, western Paraguay, and adjacent Argentina
ranges.Hylexetastes uniformis: tropical rainforest, also gallery and semi-deciduous forest locally, in the Amazon basin, south of the Amazon River, from northeastern Pará, Brazil, southwestward to western Mato Grosso, Rondônia and adjacent northeastern Bolivia (Santa Cruz)
ranges.Hylexetastes perrotii: southeastern Venezuela to the Guianas and Brazil north of the Amazon River
ranges.Hylexetastes stresemanni: tropical rainforest in the western Amazon basin from far eastern Colombia, far northeastern Ecuador and eastern Peru eastward to eastern Amazonas, Brazil, west of the Rio Negro, and southwestward along the Rio Madeira to far southeastern Peru and northwestern Bolivia (Pando)
ranges.Xiphocolaptes albicollis: humid to semi-deciduous and gallery forest in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado regions of eastern Brazil (from central Bahia southward to Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná), eastern Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina (Misiones and adjacent Corrientes)
ranges.Xiphocolaptes falcirostris: semi-deciduous woodland, Caatinga, palm woodland, and gallery forest in northeastern Brazil (northern Ceará, Piauí and adjacent Maranhão, southward to northern Minas Gerais)
ranges.Xiphocolaptes major: dry and semi-deciduous forest and woodland, gallery forest, and forested savanna from north-central Bolivia (Beni) eastward to southwestern Brazil (southern Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul), and southward across eastern Bolivia and western Paraguay to northern Argentina (to Catamarca and Santa Fe)
ranges.Xiphocolaptes promeropirhynchus: montane to lowland humid and dry forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in far southern San Luis Potosí (Mexico) southeastward across southeastern Mexico to northern Nicaragua, mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama, coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, foothills and slopes of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the Andes of Colombia and Ecuador to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz), ithe tepui region of southeastern Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, and far northern Brazil, and in Amazonia from southern Venezuela and eastern Colombia southward to southeastern Peru and northern Bolivia, and eastward across Amazonian Brazil (to eastern Pará)
ranges.Xiphorhynchus pardalotus: humid lowland and montane forest in the Orinoco basin, the tepui region of southern and eastern Venezuela, and the Guianas southward to northern Brazil, north of the Amazon River (southward to northeastern Amazonas, northern Pará and Amapá)
ranges.Xiphorhynchus ocellatus: mostly tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from southern Venezuela southward to southern Bolivia (southward to northern Chuquisaca); in Brazil eastward to the Rio Negro and Rio Tapajós, in eastern Amazonas and western Pará, and southward to Acre and Rondônia
ranges.Xiphorhynchus atlanticus: northeastern Brazil (Ceará and Paraíba to Alagoas)
ranges.Xiphorhynchus fuscus: semi-deciduous, gallery, and humid forest in the Atlantic Forest and in interior Brazil (from northern Bahia and Sergipe southward to Paraná, and northern Rio Grande do Sul), eastern Paraguay, and far northeastern Argentina (Misiones); in interior Brazil eastward to the Cerrado of eastern Goiás
ranges.Xiphorhynchus spixii: southeastern Amazonian Brazil south of the Amazon River
ranges.Xiphorhynchus elegans: mostly tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to northern Bolivia (La Paz and southern Beni), and eastward to the Amazon of Brazil, south of the Amazon River, to the Rio Tapajós in western Pará, and southward to central Mato Grosso
ranges.Xiphorhynchus triangularis: montane cloudforest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, from Yaracuy eastward to Miranda, and in the Sierra de Perijá and the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the western (southward to Valle del Cauca), central and eastern Andes of Colombia and eastern Andes of Ecuador to northern Peru (north of the Río Marañón), and from northern Peru, south and east of the Río Marañón, southeastward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Xiphorhynchus erythropygius: humid forest of lowlands to hills of Caribbean slope from San Luis Potosí to northern Oaxaca and locally on Pacific slope in Guerrero; thence both slopes of far eastern Oaxaca and southern Belize through southern Central America to western Colombia and Ecuador west of the Andes
ranges.Xiphorhynchus obsoletus: tropical rainforest in the Río Orinoco and Amazon basins from eastern Venezuela and the Guianas southwestward to eastern Colombia and eastern Ecuador, southward to northern Bolivia; in Brazil across the entire Amazon, eastward to eastern Pará, adjacent Maranhão, and western Tocantins, and southward to northern Mato Grosso
ranges.Xiphorhynchus flavigaster: deciduous forest (mostly) from lowlands to hills of southern Sonora on the Pacific side and central Tamaulipas on the Caribbean side, through Mexico including the Yucatan Peninsula (but not Cozumel), to northern Honduras, thence on Pacific slope to northwestern Costa Rica
ranges.Xiphorhynchus guttatus: humid forest in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from eastern and southern Venezuela and the Guianas southwestward to the western Amazon in eastern Colombia southward to central Bolivia, and across the entire Amazon of Brazil eastward to northern Piauí and Ceará, and southward to Goiás and northern Mato Grosso do Sul; also in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil, from Rio Grande do Norte southward to Espirito Santo
ranges.Xiphorhynchus lachrymosus: humid forest from the Caribbean lowlands of southern Nicaragua southeastward to eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia, also in the Pacific lowlands of southern Costa Rica and western Panama; in northern Colombia north to the lower Río Magdalena and southward along this river valley to Boyacá; west of the Andes southward to northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Xiphorhynchus susurrans: humid to semi-deciduous forest and woodland from the Caribbean slope of far eastern Guatemala southeastward to eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia, and in the Pacific slope of southern Costa Rica and Panama; in the lowlands and foothills of northern Colombia and western Venezuela, southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys to the headwaters (Cauca and Huila); east of the Andes, from Trinidad and Tobago westward across northern Venezuela (including Isla Margarita), to southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia (southward to Meta and Boyacá)
ranges.Dendroplex kienerii: far southeastern Colombia to northeastern Ecuador, northeastern Peru, and adjacent Brazil
ranges.Dendroplex picus: deciduous forest and woodland, gallery forest, forested savanna, arid scrub, river islands, and mangroves from south-central Panama eastward to northern Colombia, northern and central Venezuela (including Isla Margarita), Trinidad, and the Guianas, in interior Colombia southward along the Magdalena Valley (to Huila); in the Amazon basin from southern Venezuela southward to central Bolivia, and in Brazilian Amazonia southward to northern Mato Grosso do Sul; also in the Cerrado and Caatinga southward to western Goiás, and in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil southward to Espirito Santo
ranges.Campylorhamphus falcularius: southeastern Brazil (central Bahia) to eastern Paraguay and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Campylorhamphus pusillus: montane and foothill cloudforest in mountains of Costa Rica, western and eastern Panama, Sierra de Perijá, and the Andes from far southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia southward along the Andes of Colombia (in the eastern Andes mainly in the slopes of Magdalena Valley) to southwestern Ecuador and northeastern Peru (in southwestern Colombia and northwestern Ecuador down to lowlands)
ranges.Campylorhamphus probatus: tropical rainforest in the southern Amazon basin from the Rio Xingu, in western Pará, southwestward to the Rio Madeira, in northern Rondônia and Mato Grosso
ranges.Campylorhamphus multostriatus: eastern Amazonian Brazil between the Rio Xingu and Rio Tocantins
ranges.Campylorhamphus procurvoides: tropical rain orest in the Amazon basin mostly north of the Amazon River from southeastern Colombia, northeastern Peru and adjacent Ecuador eastward to northern Brazil and southern Venezuela, and northward to the Guianas and far northeastern Venezuela; south of the Amazon River in southwestern Brazil, west of the Rio Madeira, in Amazonas and Rondônia
ranges.Campylorhamphus trochilirostris: deciduous to humid forest and woodland from central Panama eastward to northern Colombia and northern Venezuela, east of the Andes southward to the llanos and foothills of the Andes of southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia, the tepui region of southern Venezuela and northern Brazil, central Colombia southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys (to Tolima and Huila); west of the Andes in far southwestern Colombia, western Ecuador, and northwestern Peru, the Amazon basin in river islands and riparian areas along the Amazon River (between Rio Negro and Rio Madeira), eastern Ecuador and eastern Peru southward to southwestern Brazil (Acre and Rondônia), northern and eastern Bolivia, and southward across the Chaco of Paraguay to northern Argentina (to Córdoba and Entre Rios), the Caatinga and Cerrado of northeastern and interior Brazil (Ceará and Piauí southward to southern Bahia, and southwestward to western Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul)
ranges.Drymornis bridgesii: southern Bolivia to central Argentina, Uruguay, western Paraguay, and southwestern Brazil
ranges.Drymotoxeres pucheranii: locally in western Andes of Colombia to southeastern Peru (Cusco)
ranges.Lepidocolaptes falcinellus: southeastern Brazil to northeastern Argentina, northeastern Uruguay, and southeastern Paraguay
ranges.Lepidocolaptes squamatus: deciduous and semi-deciduous woodland, gallery forest and humid forest in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado regions of eastern Brazil from southern Piauí southward to northern São Paulo
ranges.Lepidocolaptes angustirostris: deciduous forest and scrub, gallery and savanna forest, and palm swamps in northeastern Brazil, in Isla Marajó and river islands and riparian areas in the eastern Amazon River eastward to the Rio Tapajós in eastern Pará, and in savanna of southernmost Suriname; also in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado regions of eastern Brazil (Maranhão, Piauí, and Ceará southward to Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul, and west to southern Mato Grosso and adjacent Rondônia), Paraguay, central and eastern Bolivia, Uruguay, and western Rio Grande do Sul, southward to south-central Argentina (southward to La Pampa, northern Río Negro, and southern Buenos Aires; absent from the pampas)
ranges.Lepidocolaptes duidae: northwestern Amazonia, from Venezuela and Brazil (west of the Rio Branco and Rio Negro) westward to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru north of the Amazon
ranges.Lepidocolaptes fatimalimae: western Amazonia, south of the Amazon: eastern Peru southward to Bolivia and eastward to Brazil west of the Rio Madeira
ranges.Lepidocolaptes fuscicapillus: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin, south of the Amazon River, from northeastern Brazil (northeastern Pará) southwestward to Rondônia, southern Mato Grosso and northeastern Bolivia
ranges.Lepidocolaptes albolineatus: eastern Venezuela (Monagas and Bolívar) to the Guianas and northern Brazil (east of the Rio Branco and Rio Negro)
ranges.Lepidocolaptes souleyetii: deciduous to semi-humid forest and woodland on the Gulf of Mexico slope of southeastern Mexico (northern Oaxaca and adjacent Veracruz), and the Pacific slope (Guerrero and Oaxaca) southward across Central America to eastern Panama, northern Colombia, northern Venezuela, and Trinidad, the tepuis of southeasternmost Venezuela, adjacent Guyana, and far northern Brazil (Roraima), east of the Andes in the foothills of southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia (southward to northern Meta), in central Colombia southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys, and west of the Andes in southwestern Colombia, western Ecuador, and northwestern Peru
ranges.Lepidocolaptes lacrymiger: montane cloudforest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela (from Carabobo eastward to Sucre), Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia, through Ecuador to northwestern Peru (to Cajamarca, west of the Río Marañón), and from northern Peru east and south of the Marañón, southeastward in the eastern Andes to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Lepidocolaptes leucogaster: montane semiarid to humid forest of northeastern Sonora (northwestern Mexico) south on Pacific slope to Nayarit, thence across transvolcanic belt of Mexico and southward to south-central Oaxaca
ranges.Lepidocolaptes affinis: drier to humid montane forest of Caribbean slope from central Nuevo León and Pacific slope from Guerrero (northeastern and west-central Mexico) southward (not including Yucatan Peninsula) through northern Nicaragua and, disjunctly, northwestern Costa Rica through western Panama
ranges.Xenops tenuirostris: tropical rainforest in the Guiana Shield and Amazon basin from southern Venezuela, northernmost Brazil and the Guianas southwestward to eastern Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, and southward to northern Bolivia; in Brazil mostly in central Amazonia in Amazonas, Pará, Rondônia and Mato Grosso
ranges.Xenops rutilans: deciduous to humid forest and woodland in the mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama, also in eastern Panama and possibly adjacent Colombia; in South America, in the foothills of Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the Andes of western Venezuela, southward along the western (southward to Valle del Cauca), central, and eastern Andes of Colombia to the Andes of northwestern Argentina (southward to Tucuman); west of the Andes in the lowlands of western Ecuador and far northwestern Peru; also in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela from Lara and Falcón eastward to Monagas, and Trinidad; in Amazonia widespread south of the Amazon River from southern Amazonas southward to northern Bolivia and eastward to Maranhão, also in eastern Brazil from Ceará southward to Rio Grande do Sul, northeastern Argentina, and northern and eastern Paraguay
ranges.Xenops mexicanus: semi-deciduous to humid forest from the Gulf of Mexico slope in northern Oaxaca and southern Veracruz (Mexico), southeastward across northern Central America to Panama, also the Pacific slope of Costa Rica eastward to Panama; in South America from northern Colombia and western Venezuela southward along the Cauca and Magdalena valleys (to Valle del Cauca and Tolima), and west of the Andes southward along the Pacific lowlands of Colombia to far northwestern Peru
ranges.Xenops minutus: eastern Brazil (north to southern Bahia) to eastern Paraguay and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Xenops genibarbis: semi-humid to tropical rainforest in the Orinoco and Amazon basins and the Guiana Shield from northern Venezuela eastward to eastern Maranhão and adjacent Piaui, in northeastern Brazil, and southward across the Amazon basin to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz), and the Atlantic Forest of northeastern Brazil from Rio Grande do Norte and Paraiba southward to Sergipe
ranges.Berlepschia rikeri: southeastern Colombia to eastern Peru, northwestern Bolivia, the Guianas, and Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Microxenops milleri: southeastern Colombia to southern Venezuela, the Guianas, eastern Peru, and Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Pygarrhichas albogularis: central Chile and adjacent Argentina southward to Tierra del Fuego
ranges.Ochetorhynchus melanurus: arid montane scrub, cliffs and slopes with scattered vegetation in central-north Chile from Atacama southward to central Chile (Maule)
ranges.Ochetorhynchus andaecola: Andes of western Bolivia to northwestern Argentina and adjacent northern Chile
ranges.Ochetorhynchus phoenicurus: southern Argentina (Neuquén to southern Santa Cruz) and far southern Chile
ranges.Ochetorhynchus ruficaudus: arid montane scrub, bunch-grass, and rocky slopes in the Andes of southern Peru, from Arequipa southward across Bolivia and northeastern Chile, to the Andes of central Chile and further southward to Patagonia and Andes of southern Argentina, to northwestern Santa Cruz
ranges.Premnoplex tatei: cloudforest of Serranía de Turimiquire, Cordillera de Caripe, and mountains of Paría Peninsula (northeastern Venezuela)
ranges.Premnoplex brunnescens: montane cloudforest in the mountains of Costa Rica and Panama (including Cordillera de San Blas, Cerro Tarcarcuna, and Cerro Pirre) in eastern Panama, in South America in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela (eastward to Miranda), and in the Andes of western Venezuela southward in the Andes of Colombia to far northern Peru (including the Cordillera del Condor and the Mache Chindul mountains of northwestern Ecuador), in the eastern Andes of Peru south of the Río Marañón southward to central Bolivia (westernmost Santa Cruz)
ranges.Margarornis squamiger: montane cloudforest in the Andes from western Venezuela and the Sierra de Perijá, southward along the entire Andes of Colombia to northern Peru (to Cajamarca), north and west of the Río Marañón; and in the eastern Andes of Peru east of the Río Marañón from Amazonas southeastward to central Bolivia, to western Santa Cruz
ranges.Margarornis rubiginosus: montane evergreen forest from northwestern Costa Rica to central Panama
ranges.Margarornis stellatus: western Andes of Colombia and northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Margarornis bellulus: humid montane forest of eastern Panama (Cerro Pirre)
ranges.Cichlocolaptes mazarbarnetti: formerly northeastern Brazil; currently known from only two sites, in Alagoas and Pernambuco; extinct
ranges.Cichlocolaptes leucophrus: humid lowland and montane forest in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil, from central Bahia southward to northern Rio Grande do Sul
ranges.Heliobletus contaminatus: lowland and montane humid forest in the Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil, from southern Bahia southward to Rio Grande do Sul and adjacent Uruguay, and southwestward to northernmost Argentina (Misiones) and eastern Paraguay
ranges.Philydor pyrrhodes: southeastern Colombia to southern Venezuela, the Guianas, northern Bolivia, and eastern Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Philydor atricapillus: eastern Paraguay to southeastern Brazil (southern Bahia) and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Philydor novaesi: formerly montane forest of northeastern Brazil (Alagoas); extinction date 2011
ranges.Anabazenops fuscus: southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo to eastern Santa Catarina)
ranges.Anabazenops dorsalis: southeastern Colombia to far northwestern Bolivia and western Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Neophilydor fuscipenne: humid lowland to hill forest of central and eastern Panama to northern and north-central Colombia and, disjunctly, in western Ecuador
ranges.Neophilydor erythrocercum: tropical rainforest and humid montane forest in the Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia, and eastward across Brazilian Amazonia to northeastern Brazil (eastward to northeastern Pará and adjacent Maranhão) and northward to the Guianas
ranges.Megaxenops parnaguae: arid Caatinga of interior northeastern and east-central Brazil
ranges.Anabacerthia amaurotis: southeastern Paraguay to southeastern Brazil (southern Espírito Santo) and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Anabacerthia lichtensteini: eastern Paraguay to eastern and southeastern Brazil and northeastern Argentina (Misiones)
ranges.Anabacerthia striaticollis: montane cloudforest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela (from Yaracuy eastward to Miranda), and in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá and the Andes of western Venezuela southward along the western (southward to Valle del Cauca), central and eastern Andes of Colombia and eastern Andes of Ecuador through eastern Andes of Peru to central Bolivia (to western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Anabacerthia ruficaudata: tropical rainforest in the Río Orinoco and Amazon basins from central Venezuela and the Guianas southwestward to eastern Colombia, eastern Ecuador and Peru southward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz), and in central and eastern Amazonia in Brazil, eastward to western Maranhão and northern Tocantins, and southward to northern Mato Grosso
ranges.Anabacerthia variegaticeps: montane evergreen forest of both slopes of southern Mexico from Guerrero and central Veracruz southward (and including Sierra de las Tuxtlas), but not the Yucatan Peninsula, and southern Belize to north-central Nicaragua, and northwestern Costa Rica southward through western Panama; disjunctly, western Andes of Colombia (southward from southern Chocó) and western Ecuador including western coastal cordilleras
ranges.Syndactyla dimidiata: humid and gallery forest and woodland in the Cerrado region of interior Brazil from western Bahia and northern Goiás southward to Mato Grosso do Sul and adjacent Paraguay
ranges.Syndactyla rufosuperciliata: montane cloudforest in the Andes of far southeastern Ecuador southward along the eastern Andes of Peru to northwestern Argentina (southward to La Rioja); also in humid forest and bamboo stands in the Atlantic Forest region of southeastern Brazil, from Minas Gerais and Espirito Santo southwestward to northeastern Argentina (southward to northern Buenos Aires), Uruguay and eastern Paraguay
ranges.Syndactyla roraimae: tepuis of southern Venezuela, adjacent southwestern Guyana, and far northern Brazil (Roraima)
ranges.Syndactyla ucayalae: tropical southeastern Peru, far northwestern Bolivia, and Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Syndactyla striata: Yungas of western Bolivia (La Paz, Cochabamba, and western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Syndactyla guttulata: humid montane forest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, from Falcón eastward to Sucre and Monagas
ranges.Syndactyla subalaris: montane cloudforest in the mountains of Costa Rica, western and eastern Panama, and adjacent Colombia, and the Andes of western Venezuela, southward along the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia to far northern Peru north of the Río Marañón (Cajamarca), and the eastern Andes of Peru east and south of the Marañón, southward to southern Peru (Junín, Ucayali, and Cusco)
ranges.Ancistrops strigilatus: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from southeastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia, and eastward to the Brazilian Amazonia, mainly south of the Amazon River, to central Pará, in the Rio Tapajós region
ranges.Dendroma erythroptera: tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin from eastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia and eastward, south of the Amazon River, to northeastern Brazil (eastern Pará and adjacent Maranhão), and in Brazil southward to northern Mato Grosso; also in southern Venezuela
ranges.Dendroma rufa: humid montane forest and riparian and humid forest in the mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama; in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, in Falcón eastward to Miranda, in Colombia along the western Andes southward to western Ecuador in the central Andes of Colombia, including Sierra de San Lucas, southward to Tolima, and in the eastern Andes in northeastern Colombia, and from eastern Ecuador southward to southern Bolivia (Chuquisaca); also in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado of southeastern Brazil, from southern Bahia southward to northern Rio Grande do Sul, and westward to Goiás, southern Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, northeastern Argentina and eastern Paraguay; and in the tepuis of southern Venezuela
ranges.Clibanornis rectirostris: Campos of interior eastern and south-central Brazil to northeastern Paraguay
ranges.Clibanornis dendrocolaptoides: eastern Paraguay to southeastern Brazil and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Clibanornis rufipectus: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (northeastern Colombia)
ranges.Clibanornis erythrocephalus: deciduous to semi-deciduous forest in southwestern Ecuador (including the Chongon Colonche mountains in Manabí, Santa Elena, and Guayas), and northwestern Peru (southward to northern Lambayeque and western Cajamarca)
ranges.Clibanornis rubiginosus: humid montane and lowland forest on the Gulf of Mexico slope, from southern San Luis Potosí (Mexico), and the Pacific slope from Guerrero southeastward across Guatemala and adjacent El Salvador to northern Nicaragua, locally in eastern Costa Rica, western, central and eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia; in South America, west of the Andes from northwestern Colombia southward to southwestern Ecuador, and along the foothills of the central Andes and the western slope of the eastern Andes of Colombia (to Tolima and Cundinamarca); east of the Andes along the Andean foothills from southwestern Venezuela southward across Colombia and Ecuador to northwestern Bolivia (in Ecuador and Peru to the Amazon lowlands) and eastward to Acre and southern Amazonas (southwestern Brazil); also in southern Venezuela and the Guianas southward to northern Brazil (Roraima, Amapá, and eastern Amazonas)
ranges.Thripadectes ignobilis: humid western Andes of Colombia and western Ecuador (southward to El Oro)
ranges.Thripadectes scrutator: east slope of Andes of Peru and western Bolivia (Cochabamba)
ranges.Thripadectes flammulatus: montane cloudforest and bamboo stands in Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and in the Andes from western Venezuela southward along the western, central and eastern Andes of Colombia to far northern Peru (Cajamarca); in western Ecuador southward to Azuay
ranges.Thripadectes holostictus: montane cloudforest in the Andes from far western Venezuela southward along the western, central and eastern Andes of Colombia through Ecuador (in the western Andes of Ecuador southward to Azuay) to northern Peru (Cajamarca), north of the Río Marañón; from northern Peru (Amazonas), south and east of the Río Marañón, southeastward to central Bolivia (western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Thripadectes rufobrunneus: central highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama
ranges.Thripadectes melanorhynchus: montane and foothill cloudforest in the eastern Andes from central Colombia (Boyacá) southward to northern Peru north of the Río Marañón (Cajamarca), and from northern Peru, south and east of the Río Marañón (Amazonas and San Martin) southeastward to southeastern Peru (Puno)
ranges.Thripadectes virgaticeps: montane and foothill cloudforest in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela, in Carabobo eastward to Miranda), in the Sierra de Perijá and in the Andes of western Venezuela southward along the western, central and eastern Andes of Colombia (not in northeastern Colombia) to northern Ecuador (western Chimborazo, in the western Andes, and Tungurahua, in the eastern Andes)
ranges.Automolus melanopezus: southeastern Colombia to southeastern Peru, far northwestern Bolivia, and western Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Automolus rufipileatus: riparian and varzea forest, Gynerium thickets and bamboo stands along the foothills of the Andes of western Venezuela southward to eastern Colombia, where also descends to the Amazon lowlands, and southward across Ecuador and Peru to northwestern Bolivia and southwestern Brazil, in Acre; also in southern Venezuela and the Guianas southward to northern Brazil and the eastern Amazon of Brazil, in Pará, eastern Amazonas, eastward to westernmost Maranhão and Tocantins, and southward to northern Mato Grosso and Rondônia
ranges.Automolus infuscatus: tropical rainforest in the Río Orinoco and Amazon basins from eastern and central Venezuela, the Guianas and northeasternmost Brazil (Amapá) southwestward to the western Amazon in Brazil, eastward to the Rio Negro region (Amazonas, northern Rondônia and Acre), Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, southward to northwestern Bolivia
ranges.Automolus paraensis: Brazil south of the Amazon River (Rio Madeira to Rio Tocantins)
ranges.Automolus leucophthalmus: humid forest in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado regions of southeastern Brazil, from southern Bahia southward to northernmost Rio Grande do Sul and southwestward to Goiás and southern Mato Grosso, eastern Paraguay, and far northeastern Argentina (Misiones)
ranges.Automolus subulatus: tropical rainforest in the upper Orinoco and Amazon basins, from southern Venezuela southwestward to central and western Amazon of Brazil (from eastern Pará and southward to northern Mato Grosso and Rondônia), and from southeastern Colombia southward to northwestern Bolivia (southward to northern La Paz and adjacent Beni)
ranges.Automolus virgatus: humid forest of lowlands and foothills of southern Central America, southward from northeastern Honduras (where rare and local), on both slopes of Costa Rica, and Caribbean slope of Panama through much of central and western Colombia, thence west of the Andes to southwestern Ecuador
ranges.Automolus ochrolaemus: tropical rainforest from eastern Panama and northwestern Colombia southward along the Pacific lowlands to west-central Ecuador and southward along the Magdalena Valley (to Tolima); widespread east of the Andes in the Orinoco and Amazon basins from central and eastern Venezuela and the Guianas southward to Amazonia in eastern Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, and central Bolivia (in western Santa Cruz), and in Brazil (eastward to Amapá and central-east Pará, southward to eastern Mato Grosso)
ranges.Automolus exsertus: Pacific slope of southwestern Costa Rica to western Panama (Chiriquí)
ranges.Automolus cervinigularis: forest to plantations of lowlands and hills on Caribbean slope from central Veracruz and northern Oaxaca (southeastern Mexico) through Mexico, including the southern Yucatan Peninsula in east-central Campeche, Peten (northern Guatemala), and Belize, through northwestern Panama
ranges.Tarphonomus harterti: Andes of southern Bolivia (Cochabamba, western Santa Cruz, and Chuquisaca)
ranges.Tarphonomus certhioides: Chaco of southeastern Bolivia, western Paraguay, and northern to central Argentina
ranges.Premnornis guttuliger: montane cloudforest in the Sierra de Perijá and the Andes from far western Venezuela southward along the Andes of Colombia to northwestern Ecuador and along the eastern Andes to far southeastern Peru
ranges.Pseudocolaptes lawrencii: highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama (western Chiriquí)
ranges.Pseudocolaptes johnsoni: west slope of western Andes of southwestern Colombia and western Ecuador
ranges.Pseudocolaptes boissonneautii: deciduous woodland and Chaco scrub from southeastern Bolivia and western Paraguay southward across interior Argentina to southern Buenos Aires, Río Negro, and Mendoza; locally in far southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Lochmias nematura: rivers and streams in montane forest in the mountains of far eastern Panama and adjacent Colombia, and in the western (southward to Valle del Cauca), central (except northern), and eastern Andes of Colombia, from Cundinamarca southward across eastern Andes of Ecuador and Peru to southern Bolivia and adjacent northwestern Argentina; in the coastal mountains of northern Venezuela in Yaracuy eastward to Aragua), and in the tepuis of southern Venezuela and adjacent Guyana; also in interior and eastern Brazil from Tocantins and central Bahia southward to Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul, Uruguay, eastern Paraguay and northeastern Argentina (Misiones), and westward in Brazil to southern Mato Grosso and northern Mato Grosso do Sul
ranges.Limnornis curvirostris: far southern Brazil to southern Uruguay and eastern Argentina
ranges.Phleocryptes melanops: rushes in freshwater marshes from northwestern Peru (Piura) southward to southeastern Bolivia, northwestern Argentina and northern Chile; from western Paraguay (where seasonal) and southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro) southward across Uruguay and most Argentina and central Chile southward to southern Santa Cruz and adjacent Chile, near Tierra del Fuego
ranges.Furnarius cristatus: Chaco of southeastern Bolivia to western Paraguay and northern Argentina
ranges.Furnarius minor: Amazonian Brazil, southern Colombia, eastern Ecuador, and northeastern Peru
ranges.Furnarius rufus: open areas and secondary scrub in northeastern Brazil (from southeastern Pará, southern Maranhão, and Pernambuco), southward across the Atlantic Forest and interior Brazil to south-central Argentina (northern Chubut and Río Negro), and westward in central Brazil (Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul) to central Bolivia (west to eastern La Paz)
ranges.Furnarius figulus: riparian woodland, scrub and open-areas in the lower Amazon basin from eastern Amazonas eastward to central Pará and southward along the Rio Araguaia to northern Goiás and eastern Mato Grosso; also in eastern Brazil from northern Maranhão, Piauí, and Ceará southward to coastal Paraná and Santa Catarina, and inland to western São Paulo and adjacent Mato Grosso do Sul
ranges.Furnarius longirostris: open areas and secondary scrub in the lowlands of northeastern Colombia and northwestern Venezuela (eastward to Yaracuy and Carabobo), west to the Gulf of Uraba region (Córdoba, northern Antioquia, and Chocó), and southward along the Magdalena Valley (to Tolima and northern Huila)
ranges.Furnarius cinnamomeus: far southwestern Colombia (Nariño), western Ecuador, and northwestern Peru
ranges.Furnarius torridus: along the Amazon River (southern Colombia, northeastern Ecuador, northeastern Peru, and western Brazil)
ranges.Furnarius leucopus: open and semi-open areas, gallery forest and woodland, riparian scrub, and grassy fields from northern Brazil (Roraima) and adjacent Guyana southwestward across western Brazil (western Amazonas, Acre, and adjacent Rondônia) to far southeastern Colombia, eastern Peru and far southeastern Ecuador; to northern Bolivia, south-central Brazil (Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul), adjacent Paraguay, northeastward to eastern Brazil (to northern Maranhão, Piauí, and Ceará, and southward to Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo)
ranges.Geocerthia serrana: tall puna grassland, arid montane scrub and Polylepis woodland in the Andes from northern Peru (Cajamarca) southward to southern Peru (northeastern Ayacucho)
ranges.Upucerthia validirostris: puna grassland, arid montane scrub and woodland, gravelly streams in the Andes from northern Peru (La Libertad) southward across Bolivia and far northeastern Chile to northwestern Argentina, southward to Catamarca and patchily further southward to La Rioja and Mendoza; also isolated in the sierras of Córdoba
ranges.Upucerthia albigula: west slope of Andes of southwestern Peru and far northern Chile (Arica)
ranges.Upucerthia dumetaria: arid scrub, puna grassland, shrub-steppe, and rocky grassland in the Andes of far southeastern Peru (Puno) southward across the altiplano of Bolivia and northern Chile to the Andes of western Argentina and Chile, and southward across Patagonia to Tierra del Fuego; non-breeding migration from southern Argentina northward to the pampas of northern and northeastern Argentina and adjacent Uruguay
ranges.Cinclodes aricomae: Andes of southern Peru and far western Bolivia (La Paz)
ranges.Cinclodes excelsior: dry to humid grassy and rocky paramo and adjacent montane scrub, bogs, meadows and Polylepis woodland in the northern part of the central Andes of Colombia, in Caldas, Risaralda, and Tolima, and from southern Colombia southward to southern Ecuador, in northern Loja
ranges.Cinclodes pabsti: montane savanna with rocky outcrops and temperate grassland often near water in the highlands of southeastern Brazil, in Paraná and northern Rio Grande do Sul
ranges.Cinclodes palliatus: Andes of central Peru (Junín, Lima, and Huancavelica)
ranges.Cinclodes patagonicus: coastal rocky and short-grass areas, rocky streams, river and lake shores from central Chile and west-central Argentina (Mendoza) southward to Tierra del Fuego, including some islands
ranges.Cinclodes nigrofumosus: rocky coasts of Chile (Arica southward to Valdivia)
ranges.Cinclodes taczanowskii: rocky coasts of Peru (Ancash southward to Tacna)
ranges.Cinclodes fuscus: southern Chile and southern Argentina; winters to southeastern Brazil, Uruguay, and Paraguay
ranges.Cinclodes antarcticus: coastal rocky and short-grass and tussock areas in Tierra del Fuego of far southern Chile and southern Argentina, including offshore islands in the Cape Horn Archipelago, and the Falkland Islands
ranges.Cinclodes comechingonus: Andes of north-central Argentina (western Córdoba to eastern Tucumán)
ranges.Cinclodes albidiventris: paramo grassland and arid montane scrub in the Andes from western Venezuela and Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta southward along the eastern and central Andes of Colombia through Ecuador to northern Peru, north and west of the Río Marañón; in the western Andes of Ecuador southward to northern Loja
ranges.Cinclodes albiventris: paramo and puna grassland, arid montane scrub and fields in the Andes of northern Peru, from southern Amazonas and Cajamarca southward across Peru and Bolivia to northern Chile and northwestern Argentina (southward to La Rioja)
ranges.Cinclodes atacamensis: Andes of Peru to western Bolivia, northern Chile, and northern Argentina, and mountains of central Argentina (Sierra de Córdoba and northeastern San Luis)
ranges.Cinclodes olrogi: Andes of north-central Argentina (western Córdoba and northeastern San Luis)
ranges.Cinclodes oustaleti: open rocky and grassy areas from northern Chile and northwestern Argentina southward to Tierra del Fuego, including islands of the Cape Horn Archipelago; breeds in the Andes and migrates to the coast; also in Alejandro Selkirk Island off central Chile
ranges.Aphrastura masafuerae: Alejandro Selkirk Island (Juan Fernández Islands off Chile)
ranges.Aphrastura spinicauda: humid temperate forest and scrub in central Chile, from southern region of Coquimbo, and far western Argentina in Mendoza, southward to Tierra del Fuego including Isla de los Estados, Isla Hornos and Diego Ramirez archipelago
ranges.Sylviorthorhynchus desmurii: central and southern Chile and adjacent Argentina
ranges.Sylviorthorhynchus yanacensis: locally in Andes of central and southeastern Peru, Bolivia, and northwestern Argentina (Jujuy, Salta)
ranges.Leptasthenura xenothorax: Andes of southern Peru (Apurímac and Cusco)
ranges.Leptasthenura setaria: southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro to Rio Grande do Sul) to northeastern Argentina
ranges.Leptasthenura platensis: southern Paraguay; far southwestern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina
ranges.Leptasthenura striolata: southeastern Brazil (Paraná southward to northern Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Leptasthenura striata: arid montane scrub in the western Andes of northern Peru, from La Libertad southward to northernmost Chile, in northern region of Antofagasta; also in inter-Andean valleys of southern Peru, in Huancavelica, Ayacucho, and Apurimac
ranges.Leptasthenura pileata: Polylepis and Gynoxys woodland and adjacent scrub in the Andes from northern Peru, in southern Cajamarca, southward to southern Peru, in Arequipa
ranges.Leptasthenura fuliginiceps: arid to humid montane scrub and Polylepis woodland in the Andes from western Bolivia southward to west-central Argentina (Mendoza and the sierras of Córdoba and San Luis)
ranges.Leptasthenura aegithaloides: arid scrub, espinal, rocky slopes, forest borders, and puna grassland with bushes in the coast of southern Peru, in Arequipa, southward to southern Chile; also in the Andes from far southeast Peru southward across the Andes of Bolivia and northeastern Chile to southern Argentina, to Tierra del Fuego; southern populations migrate northward during the austral winter to north-central Argentina
ranges.Leptasthenura andicola: shrubby paramo, humid to arid montane scrub, Polylepis woodland, and treeline in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Andes of western Venezuela and the eastern Andes of Colombia (Boyacá to Cundinamarca), the central Andes of Colombia (from northern Tolima and Caldas) southward to southern Ecuador (northern Loja), and disjunctly in Zamora Chinchipe, Andean puna from northern Peru (Ancash) southeastward to southeastern Peru and adjacent western Bolivia (La Paz)
ranges.Anumbius annumbi: savanna of Paraguay to southern Brazil, Uruguay, and central Argentina
ranges.Coryphistera alaudina: arid lowland scrub, monte, and Chaco woodland from southeastern Bolivia and Paraguay southward across Argentina, western Uruguay, and southernmost Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul) to east-central Argentina, to southern Buenos Aires and adjacent La Pampa
ranges.Phacellodomus striaticeps: arid montane scrub in Andean valleys of southern Peru, in Junín southeastward to Cusco and Puno, and southward across the Andes of Bolivia to northwestern Argentina (southward to Catamarca and La Rioja)
ranges.Phacellodomus sibilatrix: Chaco of western Paraguay to southern Bolivia, western Uruguay, and northern Argentina
ranges.Phacellodomus inornatus: open woodland, savanna with scattered scrub, humid to dry and gallery forest from northeastern Venezuela, in Monagas, westward to Falcón, and southwestward to northeastern Colombia, to Meta
ranges.Phacellodomus rufifrons: arid to semi-humid woodland and scrub, Cerrado, deciduous and gallery forest, and savanna with scattered trees in southernmost Ecuador and the Marañón Valley of northern Peru (southward to San Martin), southward in the Andes of Bolivia to northwestern Argentina (southward to Catamarca), northern and eastern Bolivia eastward to western Paraguay, adjacent northern Argentina, and south-central Brazil (Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul), and in interior and eastern Brazil (northern Piauí and eastern Maranhão southward to São Paulo)
ranges.Phacellodomus erythrophthalmus: coastal eastern Brazil (southern Bahia to São Paulo)
ranges.Phacellodomus ferrugineigula: coastal southeastern Brazil (São Paulo to southern Rio Grande do Sul)
ranges.Phacellodomus ruber: northern Brazil to northern Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina
ranges.Phacellodomus striaticollis: southeastern Brazil (eastern Paraná) to Uruguay and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Phacellodomus maculipectus: Andes of southern Bolivia and northwestern Argentina (south to La Rioja)
ranges.Hellmayrea gularis: montane cloudforest in the Sierra de Perijá and Andes of western Venezuela southward along the western, central, and eastern Andes of Colombia to northernmost Peru north and west of the Río Marañón, and in the eastern Andes of Peru south of the Marañón (Amazonas southward to northern Ayacucho)
ranges.Asthenes baeri: arid scrub, monte, and Chaco woodland from southeastern Bolivia and western Paraguay southward across northern Argentina to Neuquén and Río Negro, also eastward to southernmost Brazil (in Rio Grande do Sul) and Uruguay
ranges.Asthenes huancavelicae: arid Andes of southwestern Peru (southern La Libertad to Apurímac)
ranges.Asthenes dorbignyi: Andes of northwestern Bolivia (La Paz) to northwestern Argentina
ranges.Asthenes arequipae: Andes of western Peru (southern Lima and Ayacucho) to western Bolivia and far northern Chile
ranges.Asthenes berlepschi: Andes of western Bolivia (Nevado Illampu region, Upper Río Consata drainage, in La Paz)
ranges.Asthenes luizae: east-central Brazil (Serra do Espinhaço in Minas Gerais)
ranges.Asthenes hudsoni: far southern Brazil to Uruguay and eastern Argentina (south to Río Negro)
ranges.Asthenes urubambensis: treeline, puna grassland and Polylepis woodlands in the Andes from northern Peru (southern Amazonas and adjacent San Martin) southward to central Bolivia (Cochabamba)
ranges.Asthenes flammulata: Espeletia and shrubby paramo in the eastern and central Andes of Colombia southward across Ecuador to central Peru (southward to Junín)
ranges.Asthenes virgata: very local in Andes of central and southern Peru
ranges.Asthenes maculicauda: locally in Andes of southern Peru (Puno) to western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina
ranges.Asthenes humilis: puna grassland in the Andes from northern Peru (Cajamarca) southward to southeastern Peru (Cusco and Puno) and northwestern Bolivia (southeastward to Cochabamba)
ranges.Asthenes modesta: puna and scrub of high Andes of Junín (central Peru) southward to southern Chile and Argentina; disjunctly mountains of northeastern San Luis and western Córdoba (north-central Argentina); to lowlands in Patagonia southward to Strait of Magellan
ranges.Asthenes anthoides: far southern Chile and southern Argentina to Tierra del Fuego and Staten Island
ranges.Asthenes wyatti: grassy, Espeletia, and shrubby paramo, arid montane scrub, puna grassland, and Polylepis woodland edges in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Sierra de Perijá, and the Andes of western Venezuela and northeastern Colombia (southward to Cundinamarca); in Ecuador from northern Carchi southward to northern Loja, and patchily along the Andes of Peru from Cajamarca southeastward to Bolivia and northwestern Argentina (southward to northern Mendoza) in the sierras of Córdoba and San Luis
ranges.Asthenes moreirae: high mountains of southeastern Brazil (southern Espírito Santo to northeastern São Paulo)
ranges.Asthenes heterura: Andes of western Bolivia (La Paz and Cochabamba)
ranges.Asthenes pyrrholeuca: arid scrub, shrub-steppe, and temperate grassland in north-central Argentina and north-central Chile southward to southern Argentina and Chile near Tierra del Fuego; migrates northward during austral winter to northern Argentina, Uruguay, southern Paraguay, and southeastern Bolivia
ranges.Asthenes griseomurina: Andes of southern Ecuador and far northern Peru
ranges.Asthenes coryi: Andes of western Venezuela (northern Táchira, Mérida, and Trujillo)

ranges.Asthenes helleri: Andes of southern Peru (southern Cusco and Puno)
ranges.Asthenes harterti: Andes of western Bolivia (La Paz, Cochabamba, and western Santa Cruz)
ranges.Asthenes ottonis: Andes of central Peru (Huancavelica to Cusco)
ranges.Asthenes pudibunda: arid woodland and shrubs in the Andes from northern Peru (La Libertad) southward to northernmost Chile
ranges.Spartonoica maluroides: far southern Brazil to Uruguay and central Argentina
ranges.Pseudoseisura cristata: arid northeastern Brazil (Pernambuco, Piauí, Bahia, and Minas Gerais)
ranges.Pseudoseisura unirufa: eastern Bolivia, Chaco of northern Paraguay, and southwestern Brazil (Mato Grosso)
ranges.Pseudoseisura lophotes: southeastern Bolivia to western Paraguay, southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina
ranges.Acrobatornis fonsecai: southeastern Bahia and far northeastern Minas Gerais, eastern Brazil
ranges.Metopothrix aurantiaca: tropical southeastern Colombia to northern Bolivia and western Amazonian Brazil
ranges.Xenerpestes singularis: locally in foothills of eastern Ecuador and northern Peru
ranges.Xenerpestes minlosi: humid forest in low hills of Darién (eastern Panama) east through Caribbean lowlands of Colombia eastward to middle Magdalena Valley of central Colombia and southward in western Colombia to northwestern Ecuador
ranges.Siptornis striaticollis: local in humid hill and montane forest on southeastern Andes of Colombia to north and west of the Río Marañón in Cajamarca (northern Peru)
ranges.Roraimia adusta: tepuis of southern Venezuela, adjacent southwestern Guyana, and northern Brazil
ranges.Thripophaga gutturata: southern Colombia to northern Bolivia, the Guianas, and northern Amazonian Brazil

ranges.Thripophaga cherriei: upper Río Orinoco in eastern Colombia (eastern Vichada and eastern Guainía) and western Venezuela (northwestern Amazonas)
ranges.Thripophaga amacurensis: northeastern Venezuela (southern portion of the Río Orinoco delta)
ranges.Limnoctites rectirostris: far southern Brazil to southern Uruguay and eastern Argentina
ranges.Limnoctites sulphuriferus: southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul) to Uruguay and eastern Argentina
ranges.Cranioleuca berlepschi: Andes of northern Peru (Amazonas to La Libertad)
ranges.Cranioleuca albiceps: montane cloudforest, elfin forest and treeline in the Andes of far southeastern Peru (Pasco) and Bolivia, southeastward to westernmost Santa Cruz
ranges.Cranioleuca marcapatae: southern Peru in Vilcanota and Carabaya Ranges (Cusco)

ranges.Cranioleuca vulpina: riparian woodland, scrub and thickets, gallery forest and river islands from the lower Río Orinoco in northeastern Venezuela southwestward to the llanos of western and southwestern Venezuela and northeastern Colombia (southward to Guaviare); along the Amazon River from far eastern Peru and southeastern Colombia eastward across Brazil to Pará, northward to northern Roraima and adjacent Guyana, and more widespread south of the Amazon River in central and eastern Brazil, eastward to Piauí, northern and western Bahia, and southeastward to São Paulo and northern Paraná; in central Brazil also southward to Acre, Rondônia and southern Mato Grosso, to southeastern Peru (Ucayali), northern Bolivia (southward to northwestern Santa Cruz and adjacent Cochabamba), and far northern Paraguay

ranges.Cranioleuca muelleri: lower Amazonian Brazil and Mexiana Island
ranges.Cranioleuca pallida: mountains of southeastern Brazil (Brasília to Espírito Santo and southeastern São Paulo)
ranges.Cranioleuca obsoleta: eastern Paraguay to southeastern Brazil (São Paulo) and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Cranioleuca henricae: Andes of northern Bolivia (Río La Paz drainage system)
ranges.Cranioleuca pyrrhophia: deciduous forest, semi-deciduous, to arid scrub and woodland from the eastern foothills of the Andes of central Bolivia (La Paz and Cochabamba), southeastward to the Chaco of southestern Bolivia, western Paraguay, and northern Argentina (to northern Neuquén and Río Negro and southern Buenos Aires); eastward to southernmost Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul), and Uruguay

ranges.Cranioleuca demissa: tepuis of southern Venezuela, adjacent Guyana, and northern Brazil (northern Roraima)
ranges.Cranioleuca hellmayri: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (northeastern Colombia)
ranges.Cranioleuca semicinerea: deciduous to semi-deciduous forest from northeastern Brazil, in Ceará, southwestward across interior Brazil to northern Minas Gerais and central Goiás
