ranges.Ploceus nigricollis: lowland to montane wooded savanna, gallery forest, farmbush, and plantations, from Cameroon eastward to southwestern Ethiopia, Kenya, and southern Somalia, southward to northwestern Angola and southern Tanzania
ranges.Pachyphantes superciliosus: patchy in lowland to foothill savanna, tall grassland, farmbush, forest edge, and coffee plantations, from southwestern Senegal and Guinea-Bissau eastward through northern Cameroon to southeastern Sudan and Ethiopia, and southward to northern Angola, far northern Zambia, northwestern Tanzania, and western Kenya
ranges.Quelea quelea: grassland with sparse bushes, dry thornvelds and semiarid scrub south of the Sahara from southern Mauritania and southwestern Mali eastward to southern Sudan and western Eritrea, thence southward through eastern Africa to southern South Africa; more patchily in western Africa in southern Cameroon and from Gabon southward to South Africa
ranges.Quelea erythrops: lowland to foothill savanna, grassland, and cultivation, from Senegambia and Mali eastward though Cameroon and São Tomé (Gulf of Guinea) to western Ethiopia, and southward to Angola, Zambia, Mozambique, and southeastern South Africa; some populations intra-African migrants; extirpated in Príncipe (Gulf of Guinea) but recently reintroduced there
ranges.Quelea cardinalis: patchy in foothill to montane dry wooded grassland and rank vegetation from South Sudan and western Ethiopia southward to eastern Zambia and Malawi; seasonal dispersal after rains
ranges.Foudia rubra: uplands of southwestern Mauritius (western Mascarene Islands)
ranges.Foudia eminentissima: evergreen forest in the Comoros Islands, including Mayotte
ranges.Foudia madagascariensis: Madagascar; introduced Réunion, Mauritius, Seychelles, Rodrigues, Amirantes, and Chagos Islands (Indian Ocean); also on St. Helena (Atlantic Ocean); and Bahrain (Arabian Peninsula); present also on Glorieuses and Comoro islands (Indian Ocean)
ranges.Euplectes aureus: lowland grassland, open acacia savanna, and farmbush in coastal west-central Angola; presumably introduced to São Tomé (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Euplectes afer: patchy in lowland to foothill grassland and seasonal swamps from southern Mauritania eastward to southern Sudan and central Ethiopia, southward to northern Namibia and Zimbabwe, thence southward to Lesotho and eastern South Africa, seasonally nomadic with rains; introduced on Iberian Peninsula, Jamaica, and some eastern Caribbean islands
ranges.Euplectes gierowii: very patchily distributed in lowland to montane grassland, bush, and swamp from Cameroon and western Central African Republic eastward to western Ethiopia, and southward to northwestern Angola and central Tanzania
ranges.Euplectes franciscanus: lowland to montane tall or brushy grassland, seasonally flooded wetland, and cultivation, from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward through Sahel to Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, and southward to southern Nigeria, Uganda, and western Kenya; introduced in Puerto Rico
ranges.Euplectes ardens: patchy in lowland to submontane open or sparsely-wooded grassland, cultivation, farmbush, and forest clearings, from Guinea (possibly Senegal) and southern Mali eastward to northern Uganda and southeastern Kenya, and southward to northern Angola, Zimbabwe, and eastern South Africa
ranges.Euplectes laticauda: patchy in foothill and montane grassland, wooded savanna, and open bush in eastern South Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, and in western and central Kenya and northern Tanzania
ranges.Euplectes orix: lowland to foothill grassland, farmbush, and cultivation, from northern Angola eastward to southern Uganda and southern Kenya, and southward to South Africa; introduced to United Arab Emirates
ranges.Euplectes nigroventris: lowland to foothill coastal grassland and cultivation from southeastern Kenya and eastern Tanzania, including Pemba and Unguja (Zanzibar), and southward to southwestern Tanzania and northern Mozambique; escapees reported Singapore
ranges.Euplectes diadematus: lowland to foothill grassland, bushy coastal dunes, cultivation, and seasonally flooded wetlands, from central Kenya eastward to southern Somalia, and southward to southeastern Kenya and adjacent far northeastern Tanzania; migratory or nomadic dispersal related to rains
ranges.Euplectes hordeaceus: lowland to submontane savanna, tall grassland, cultivation, farmbush, and seasonal wetland, from southern Mauritania and Mali eastward to southern Sudan and Ethiopia, and southward through Democratic Republic of the Congo and Tanzania, including Pemba and Unguja (Zanzibar), to Angola, northern and eastern Zimbabwe, and central Mozambique; introduced to São Tomé (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Euplectes anomalus: patchy in lowland grassy clearings in forest near major rivers from southeastern Cameroon, southwestern Central African Republic, and northern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and southward to far western and central Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Angola
ranges.Euplectes albonotatus: lowland and foothill bushed grassland from Central African Republic eastward through southern Sudan to Ethiopia, southward to Angola, northeastern Namibia, northern Botswana, and Zimbabwe, thence southward to southern Mozambique and eastern South Africa; introduced to São Tomé
ranges.Euplectes axillaris: patchy in sub-Saharan Africa (avoiding rainforest and southwest Africa), in grassland from southern Mali eastward to South Sudan, thence southward to northeastern Namibia and northwestern Botswana, and from western Ethiopia and southern Somalia southward through east Africa, including Pemba and Unguja (in Zanzibar, Tanzania), to southern Mozambique and eastern South Africa
ranges.Euplectes macroura: lowland to montane grasslands and wooded swamps from Senegal eastward to southern Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, southward to Angola, Zambia, Malawi, eastern Zimbabwe, and adjacent Mozambique
ranges.Euplectes capensis: patchy in lowland to montane grassland and Fynbos from southeastern Nigeria to southern Cameroon and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and from Ethiopia and southern South Sudan southward to southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, and Mozambique, and thence southward to Lesotho and southern and eastern South Africa
ranges.Euplectes hartlaubi: lowland and foothill swampy grassland from southeastern Nigeria and Cameroon eastward (except Congolian rainforest), to Uganda and western Kenya, and southward to western Angola, thence eastward to Zambia and southwestern Tanzania
ranges.Euplectes jacksoni: foothill to montane open grassland in southwestern Kenya highlands and adjacent northeastern Tanzania
ranges.Euplectes psammacromius: submontane to montane short grassland, often near streams, in southwestern Tanzania highlands, far northeastern Zambia, and northern Malawi
ranges.Euplectes progne: disjunctly in lowland to highland short-grass and coastal grassland, in central Kenya, and from Angola eastward to northeastern Zambia, and from southeastern Botswana to southern Mozambique, eastern South Africa, Lesotho, and Eswatini
ranges.Anaplectes jubaensis: patchy in lowland coastal bush and moist woodland in southern coastal Somalia and far northern coastal Kenya
ranges.Anaplectes rubriceps: lowland to montane bushveld, acacia savanna, broadleaf and miombo woodland, from Senegambia eastward across the Sahel to Ethiopia and western Somalia, southward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to northern Namibia and Mozambique, and thence southward to Eswatini and northeastern South Africa
ranges.Malimbus coronatus: patchy in lowland primary forest, mature secondary forest, and swamp-forest, from western and southern Cameroon and Gabon eastward to central and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Malimbus nitens: lowland to foothill primary and secondary forest, and swamp-forest with palms, from southwestern Senegal and Guinea-Bissau eastward to southwestern South Sudan, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and far western Uganda, and southward to Cabinda (northwestern Angola) and northeastern Angola
ranges.Malimbus malimbicus: lowland and foothill primary and old secondary rainforest and plantations, from southeast Guinea and Sierra Leone eastward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Uganda, and southward to northwestern Angola
ranges.Malimbus racheliae: lowland primary forest and adjacent parasol tree woodland, from southeastern Nigeria and southwestern Cameroon, and southward to northern Gabon
ranges.Malimbus ballmanni: disjunctly in lowland primary and old secondary forest in eastern Sierra Leone and adjacent western Liberia; far southeastern Guinea, and eastern Liberia and adjacent western Ivory Coast
ranges.Malimbus cassini: lowland to foothill tall primary forest, and swamp-forest, often with palms, from southern Cameroon eastward to northern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and southward to far western and central Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Malimbus scutatus: lowland and foothill Upper Guinea rainforest, plantations, and secondary forest, from southeast Guinea and Sierra Leone eastward to southwestern Cameroon
ranges.Malimbus rubricollis: lowland to montane primary and transitional forest from Guinea (reported Guinea-Bissau) eastward to southern Central Africa Republic, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), southward to northwestern Angola, and from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southern South Sudan, and Uganda eastward to far western Kenya and northwestern Tanzania
ranges.Malimbus erythrogaster: southeastern Nigeria eastward to far western Uganda and southward to Gabon and east-central Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Malimbus ibadanensis: very local in lowland forest-savanna mosaic, dense secondary forest edge, farmbush in degraded forests, and parkland in southwestern Nigeria
ranges.Anomalospiza imberbis: patchily distributed Sierra Leone and southern Mali eastward to Ethiopia and southward to Angola and eastern South Africa
ranges.Vidua paradisaea: lowland to foothill open woodland, miombo woodland, acacia savanna, and fallow cultivation, from southern Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia southward to eastern Rwanda and Tanzania, and from Angola eastward to Malawi and Mozambique, thence southward to northern Namibia, Botswana, and eastern South Africa
ranges.Vidua obtusa: lowland to foothill miombo woodland, grassy riverine woodland, and fallow cultivation, from northern Angola to Democratic Republic of the Congo, southwestern Uganda, Kenya, and northeastern South Africa
ranges.Vidua togoensis: lowland open woodland and old cultivation from southern Guinea and Sierra Leone eastward to Togo, and disjunctly in south-central Mali, northern Benin, and western Cameroon
ranges.Vidua interjecta: lowland to foothill open woodland, tall grassland with scattered trees, and brushy rocky hillsides, from Senegambia eastward through central Nigeria to southern South Sudan,southeastern Sudan, and eastern Ethiopia
ranges.Vidua orientalis: lowland acacia savanna and open woodland across Sahel from southern Mauritania, Senegal, and Gambia eastward through northern Cameroon, Central African Republic, and South Sudan, to Eritrea and western Ethiopia
ranges.Vidua macroura: lowland to montane grassy and shrubby savanna, marsh, cultivation, disturbed clearings, and villages, widespread sub-Saharan Africa, from southern Mauritania eastward to Sudan and Eritrea, and southward to South Africa, including São Tomé, Príncipe, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and Pemba and Unguja (in Zanzibar, Tanzania); introduced to Hawaii, southern California, Florida, Puerto Rico, and escapees elsewhere
ranges.Vidua hypocherina: lowland to foothill thornscrub, and grassland with acacia thickets, from southern South Sudan, central Ethiopia, and Somalia southward to central Tanzania
ranges.Vidua regia: lowland to foothill semiarid grassy thornscrub, acacia savanna, and fallow cultivation, from southern Angola eastward through southwestern Zambia to southern Mozambique, and southward to central Namibia, Botswana, and northern South Africa; some post-breeding nomadic dispersal
ranges.Vidua fischeri: lowland to foothill short-grass savanna, and arid thornscrub with patches of open ground, from southern South Sudan, southern Ethiopia, and Somalia, southward to central Tanzania; some post-breeding nomadic dispersal
ranges.Vidua chalybeata: widespread in sub-Saharan Africa in lowland and foothill savanna, thornscrub, mopane woodland, and cultivated land from Mauritania and Senegal eastward across the Sahel to Sudan, Ethiopia, and western Somalia, and southward (avoiding Upper Guinea and Congolian rainforest) to central Namibia, northern Botswana, and Mozambique, thence southward to eastern and central South Africa, plus Lesotho and Eswatini, but avoiding the Namib and Kalahari deserts
ranges.Vidua codringtoni: patchy and local in lowland riverine thickets, dense thicket in acacia woodland, and in village gardens, from southern and southeastern Tanzania southward to Zimbabwe and southern Mozambique
ranges.Vidua purpurascens: patchy in lowland and foothill grassy woodland, brushy grassland, riparian scrub, and thornscrub, from Kenya and Tanzania southward to northeastern Namibia, Botswana, and northeastern South Africa, and disjunctly in western Angola
ranges.Vidua funerea: lowland to montane woodland, riverine forest, and gardens from northern Kenya and Tanzania, and from northern Angola and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southward through Zambia, Mozambique, and eastern Zimbabwe to southern and eastern South Africa and Eswatini
ranges.Vidua wilsoni: lowland to foothill wooded savanna, tall grassland, fallow cultivation, villages, and gardens, from Senegambia and northern Guinea eastward to western Ethiopia, and southward to coastal Ghana, southern Nigeria, and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Vidua nigeriae: patchy and local in lowland to foothill brushy grassland, grassy floodplain, fish farms, rice fields, and cultivation, from southern Mali eastward to southern South Sudan; old records from Gambia
ranges.Vidua maryae: very local in foothill arid bushy savanna with rocky outcrops and inselbergs on Jos Plateau (central Nigeria) and disjunctly in northern Cameroon
ranges.Vidua raricola: patchy and local in lowland to foothill grassy wetland, floodplain, rice and manioc fields, and cultivation, from Sierra Leone eastward through northern Cameroon to western Ethiopia, and southward to South Sudan and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Vidua larvaticola: patchy and local in lowland to foothill bushy grassland, fallow cultivation, riverine thickets, and wooded savanna, from Guinea-Bissau and northeastern Ivory Coast eastward to southern Sudan and western Ethiopia
ranges.Vidua camerunensis: patchy and local in foothill riparian woodland, riverine scrub, and grassy or rocky cultivation, from Guinea-Bissau and southern Mali eastward to southern South Sudan and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and disjunctly southward to eastern Republic of the Congo
ranges.Heteromunia pectoralis: northern Australia (mainly Kimberley region, northern Western Australia, eastward to northwestern Queensland, but ranges to Pilbara Region and southwestern Cape York Peninsula)
ranges.Oreostruthus fuliginosus: high montane west-central to southeastern New Guinea
ranges.Stagonopleura guttata: southeastern Australia (central Queensland coast to Eyre Peninsula)
ranges.Stagonopleura oculata: southwestern Australia (Avon Valley to Cape Arid, Western Australia)
ranges.Neochmia phaeton: northern Australia and south-central New Guinea
ranges.Neochmia temporalis: eastern Australia; introduced to the Society and Marquesas islands (French Polynesia)
ranges.Emblema pictum: northern Australia (Pilbara region, including Barrow Island, central Western Australia, eastward to northwestern Queensland)
ranges.Emblema modestum: eastern Australia (northern Queensland to central New South Wales)
ranges.Spermestes griseicapilla: lowland to foothill semiarid acacia thornscrub, grassland, and open woodland, from southern Ethiopia and southeastern South Sudan southward to northeastern and central Tanzania; dispersive wandering post-breeding
ranges.Spermestes cucullata: widespread sub-Saharan Africa (except southwest Africa), from Senegal eastward to central Ethiopia, southward to northern Namibia, and southward through Tanzania, including Pemba and Unguja (in Zanzibar) and Mafia Island, to Malawi, and thence southward to southeastern Botswana, southern Mozambique, and eastern South Africa, and Comoro Islands; introduced to Gulf of Guinea islands, western South Africa, Puerto Rico, and Hawaiian islands
ranges.Spermestes fringilloides: patchy in lowland to foothill brushy grassland near rivers, riparian woodland, bamboo thickets, forest edge, and cultivation, from Senegambia and southern Mali eastward to western Ethiopia, and southward to northeastern Namibia, Zimbabwe, southern Mozambique, and eastern South Africa; erratic wandering associated with bamboo
ranges.Spermestes bicolor: widespread sub-Saharan Africa (except Congolian rainforest and southwest Africa), in lowland to montane wooded marshland, secondary growth, and abandoned cultivation from southwestern Senegal eastward to western Central African Republic, and southward to northwestern Angola and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and from western Ethiopia and southern Somalia southward to southern Mozambique and eastern South Africa
ranges.Euodice malabarica: Arabian Peninsula to southeastern Iran, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Sikkim
ranges.Euodice cantans: lowland and foothill savanna, acacia grassland, and thornscrub, from southern Mauritania eastward through the Sahel to northern Sudan (has occurred southeastern Egypt), Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, and southward to northern Tanzania, and southern Arabian Peninsula; population in southern Algeria is of origin uncertain, introduced to Hawaiian islands
ranges.Padda oryzivora: Java and Bali (where now rare); introduced widely, including St. Helena (south Atlantic), Pemba and Unjuga (Zanzibar), United Arab Emirates, Bangkok (Thailand), Malayan Peninsula, northern Borneo, Taiwan, Philippines, Fiji, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico
ranges.Mayrimunia leucosticta: lowlands of southern New Guinea (Lorentz River eastward at least to the Kikori River region, and perhaps farther eastward)
ranges.Mayrimunia tristissima: edge and cultivation of lowlands and hills of northern New Guinea, through central part of southeastern peninsula; includes Karkar Island (just off east-central New Guinea) and Umboi Island
ranges.Lonchura punctulata: northern Pakistan southward to Sri Lanka, southern China (including Hainan), Taiwan, Malayan Peninsula, Indonesian Archipelago except most of Borneo, and Philippines; introduced widely, including Portugal, southeastern Arabian Peninsula, Mauritius, Réunion, Ryukyu Islands, Yap, coastal eastern Australia, Hawaii, California, Gulf coast of USA, Caribbean
ranges.Lonchura kelaarti: semi-humid forest edges and adjacent clearings in the northern Eastern Ghats of eastern India from northern Odisha southwards to northern Andhra Pradesh, and in the Western Ghats in southwestern India from Maharashtra southwards to southern Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and in southern Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu (Peninsular India); also in highlands of Sri Lanka
ranges.Lonchura molucca: lowlands of Wallacea (except for Lesser Sundas)
ranges.Lonchura fuscans: Borneo (including Banggi, off northeastern Borneo), and Cagayan Sulu Island (in far southwestern Philippines); status on Natuna Islands unclear
ranges.Lonchura striata: lowland to submontane grassland, open shrubbery, forest edge, village gardens, and rice fields, in northwestern India from Uttarakhand eastward through Himalayan foothills to southeastern China (including Hainan), and Taiwan, and southward to Peninsular India, Sri Lanka, Andaman and Nicobar islands, Malayan Peninsula, and Sumatra and satellite islands; introduced central Ryukyu Islands (southern Japan)
ranges.Lonchura leucogastroides: lowlands of southern Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Lombok; introduced to some nearby islands
ranges.Lonchura leucogastra: lowland to foothill forest edge, peat-swamp forest, secondary growth, wet grassland, and rice fields, from Malayan Peninsula eastward to Philippines, and southward to Borneo, Sumatra, and western Java
ranges.Lonchura malacca: Peninsular India and Sri Lanka; introduced widely in Caribbean and northern South America
ranges.Lonchura ferruginosa: lowland grasslands of Java and Bali (scarce)
ranges.Lonchura atricapilla: lowland to foothill grassland, marsh, mangroves, rice paddies, and gardens, from northern India eastward to southeastern China (including Hainan), and Taiwan, southward to Philippines, Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, and satellite islands; introduced to Ryukyu Islands (southern Japan), Hong Kong, Moluccas, Palau, Vanuatu, Hawaiian Islands (all main islands), Jamaica, Martinique, and central Colombia
ranges.Lonchura pallida: scrub, marshes and ricefields of lowlands of mainland Sulawesi and the Lesser Sundas from Lombok eastward through Babar
ranges.Lonchura maja: Malayan Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, and southern Vietnam; introduced Taiwan and Hong Kong
ranges.Lonchura monticola: southwestern New Guinea (Wharton and Owen Stanley mountains)
ranges.Lonchura montana: western New Guinea (Snow Mountains) and Mount Capella (Papua New Guinea)
ranges.Lonchura teerinki: grassy and weedy areas of mountains of central West Papua (west-central New Guinea)
ranges.Lonchura flaviprymna: northwestern Australia (northeastern Kimberley region, northern Western Australia, eastward to northwestern Northern Territory)
ranges.Lonchura nevermanni: New Guinea (Kurik and Mapa areas to lower Fly River)
ranges.Lonchura melaena: lowland wet grassy areas of New Ireland and New Britain (eastern Bismarck Archipelago), and Buka (northern Solomon Islands)
ranges.Lonchura castaneothorax: northern and eastern Australia; introduced locally from New Caledonia eastward through the Marquesas Islands (eastern French Polynesia)
ranges.Lonchura grandis: local, in grassy areas of lowlands and mountains from north-central (Jayapura area) through the north and in the southeastern peninsula (north-central to southeastern New Guinea)
ranges.Lonchura caniceps: grassy areas and gardens from lowlands to mountains in southeastern peninsula of New Guinea
ranges.Lonchura spectabilis: grassy areas of lowlands and mountains from north-central (Jayapura area) through Huon Peninsula and just to the south (north-central to east-central New Guinea); also New Britain and satellite islands (southeastern Bismarck Archipelago)
ranges.Chloebia gouldiae: northern Australia (Kimberley region, northern Western Australia, to Cape York Peninsula); formerly Wet Tropics region
ranges.Erythrura kleinschmidti: montane forest of Viti Levu (northwestern Fiji)
ranges.Erythrura prasina: irruptive in bamboo, edge, and rice fields from northern Thailand southward through the Malayan Peninsula and southern Vietnam and Greater Sundas
ranges.Erythrura hyperythra: disjunctly in foothill to montane bamboo thickets, evergreen forest edge, grassland, and rice fields, on Malayan Peninsula, northern Philippines (Luzon and Mindoro), highland Borneo, Sulawesi, and patchily from Java eastward through Lesser Sundas to Flores
ranges.Erythrura pealii: Fiji (Viti Levu, Kadavu, Vanua Levu, and Taveuni)
ranges.Erythrura tricolor: Lesser Sundas (Timor, Wetar, Babar, Damar, Romang, and Tanimbar)
ranges.Erythrura papuana: mountains of New Guinea (Bird's Head Peninsula to southeastern ranges)
ranges.Erythrura trichroa: Sulawesi, Moluccas, New Guinea and associated islands, northeastern Australia (Wet Tropics), Bismarck Archipelago, Vanuatu and Loyalty Islands (Lifou and Maré, New Caledonia), Solomon Islands, and Caroline Islands
ranges.Nesocharis ansorgei: disjunctly in foothill to submontane papyrus swamps, marshy forest edge, and lakeshore thickets, in Albertine Rift from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward to western Uganda and northwestern Tanzania, and in southwestern Republic of the Congo and northwestern Angola
ranges.Nesocharis shelleyi: foothill and montane forest and cocoa plantations from southeastern Nigeria and western Cameroon southward to southern Cameroon (Mount Kupe, Mount Cameroon), and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Coccopygia quartinia: foothill and montane undergrowth, forest edge, rocky scrub or dense grass, from Eritrea and Ethiopia southward through east Africa to eastern Zimbabwe and adjacent Mozambique
ranges.Coccopygia melanotis: lowland to foothill open and brushy grassland, coastal scrub, and farmbush, from eastern and south-central Zimbabwe southward to eastern and southern South Africa, Lesotho, Eswatini, and adjacent southern Mozambique
ranges.Coccopygia bocagei: foothill and submontane tall grassland, forest edge understory, and riverine woodland, in west-central Angola
ranges.Mandingoa nitidula: patchy in lowland to montane undergrowth, evergreen scrub, and bamboo thickets, from Sierra Leone eastward to western Central African Republic, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and southward to northern Angola and northwestern Zambia, and from central Ethiopia southward to southern Mozambique and eastern South Africa
ranges.Cryptospiza shelleyi: local and declining in foothill to montane forest understory, riverine scrub, and bamboo thickets, in Albertine Rift in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southwestern Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi
ranges.Cryptospiza jacksoni: foothill to montane forest understory, bamboo thickets, riverine scrub, and forest clearings, in Albertine Rift in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southwestern Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi
ranges.Cryptospiza reichenovii: disjunctly in foothill and sub-montane thickets and dense undergrowth of highland forest, from southeastern Nigeria, adjacent Cameroon, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), in northwestern Angola (Gabela region), and from the Albertine Rift of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Uganda, southward to Burundi, and from northern Tanzania southward to eastern Zimbabwe
ranges.Cryptospiza salvadorii: patchy in montane forest undergrowth, bamboo thickets, and bracken briar, from southern South Sudan and central Ethiopia southward through Uganda and the Rwenzori Mountains to Burundi, and from central Kenya southward to northern Tanzania
ranges.Parmoptila rubrifrons: patchy in lowland and secondary forest understory, often near swampy areas, from Sierra Leone and southeastern Guinea eastward to southern Ghana
ranges.Parmoptila jamesoni: patchy in foothill primary and logged forest, often near swamps, and gallery forestunderstory, in northwestern, north-central, and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and eastward to western Uganda, and far northwestern Tanzania
ranges.Parmoptila woodhousei: patchy in lowland primary and secondary rainforest, and gallery forest, from southern Nigeria, southern Cameroon and Gabon eastward to western Central African Republic, western Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northern Angola
ranges.Nigrita fusconotus: lowland and foothill rainforest, and cocoa or palm plantations, from Sierra Leone and Guinea eastward through southern Cameron and central and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to Uganda and western Kenya, and southward to northern Angola, Rwanda, and Burundi, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Nigrita bicolor: lowland and foothill rainforest, open woodland, and wooded savanna from southwestern Senegal eastward to southern Cameroon and western Central African Republic, and southward to western Democratic Republic of the Congo and northwestern Angola, and Príncipe (Gulf of Guinea), and in the Albertine Rift mountains of northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Uganda
ranges.Nigrita luteifrons: lowland forest clearings and secondary growth from eastern Sierra Leone and Liberia eastward to southern Central African Republic, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and western Uganda, and southward to northwestern Angola and southwestern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Nigrita canicapillus: patchy from lowland and montane rainforest, gallery forest, and highland plantations from Guinea and Sierra Leone eastward to southern South Sudan, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, central Kenya, and northern Tanzania, and southward to northwestern Angola, southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and western Tanzania (Mount Kungwe)
ranges.Delacourella capistrata: patchy in lowland to foothill forest edge, grassy and and riparian woodland, often near swamps, and grassy savanna, from Guinea Bissau, Guinea, and southwestern Mali eastward through Central African Republic to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Uganda
ranges.Brunhilda erythronotos: patchy in lowland to foothill acacia scrub and riverine thickets in arid country, from western Uganda and southwestern Kenya southward to northern and central Tanzania, and from southern Angola and Namibia eastward through southwestern Zambia and Botswana to western Zimbabwe and northern South Africa
ranges.Brunhilda charmosyna: lowland and foothill acacia thickets and thornscrub from central Ethiopia and western Somalia southward to northern Uganda and central and southeastern Kenya
ranges.Glaucestrilda caerulescens: lowland to foothill open dry woodland, dense thickets, rank grassland, rocky hillsides, and margins of cultivation, from Senegambia, northern Guinea, and southern Mali eastward to southern Chad and northern Central African Republic; introduced locally in Hawaii, to Oahu and the island of Hawaii
ranges.Glaucestrilda thomensis: lowland and foothill riverine thicket in acacia and mopane woodland in western Angola and far northwestern Namibia
ranges.Glaucestrilda perreini: patchy in lowland to sub-montane open woodland or miombo, evergreen forest, bamboo and thickets from southern Gabon and Republic of the Congo southward to Angola and western and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and from southern Tanzania southward to northern and eastern South Africa, Eswatini, and southern Mozambique
ranges.Estrilda nonnula: patchy in central Africa, in lowland to montane second-growth woodland, grassy forest edge, and gardens from southeastern Nigeria, Cameroon, and central Central African Republic, and southward to Gabon, and from southern South Sudan, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and western Kenya, southward to Burundi and northwestern Tanzania, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea)
ranges.Estrilda kandti: patchy in submontane to montane forest edge and clearings, bamboo thickets, and bare rocky slopes, from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward to central Kenya, and southward to Rwanda and Burundi
ranges.Estrilda atricapilla: patchy in central Africa, in lowland forest clearings with tall grass and sedges, and villages (but avoiding Congolian rainforest), from southern Cameroon to northern Angola and southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and adjacent Uganda
ranges.Estrilda melpoda: lowland to foothill grassland, forest edge, grassy woodland, plantations, and cultivation, from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward through southern Chad and northern Democratic Republic of the Congo to western Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi, and southward to northern Angola and northern Zambia; introduced to Spain, Singapore, Taiwan, Northern Mariana Islands (Saipan and Tinian), Hawaiian Islands (Oahu and Maui), and Caribbean (Puerto Rico, Guadeloupe, and Martinique)
ranges.Estrilda poliopareia: disjunctly in lowland tall grass and sedge on sandy riverbanks, swamps, and estuaries, and in plantations, of coastal Benin and southern Nigeria
ranges.Estrilda paludicola: patchy in lowland to montane grassy woodland, tall grass, and forest edge, from Central African Republic eastward to southern Sudan and western Ethiopia, and southward from Gabon southward to western Angola, and from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southern South Sudan, and western Kenya southward to south-central Tanzania and northern Zambia
ranges.Estrilda nigriloris: patchy in lowland to foothill tall grassland and bushy savanna in south-central Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Estrilda astrild: widespread in sub-Saharan Africa (but avoiding rainforest and patchy in arid southwestern Africa), in lowland to montane grassland, acacia savanna, and grassy marsh, from Guinea, Sierra Leone, and southern Mali eastward to Eritrea, Ethiopia, and southern Somali, thence southward from Cameroon to Namibia, and from southern South Sudan to central Kenya and southward to South Africa and southern Mozambique; introduced widely, mostly on islands in tropical oceans, but also Iberian Peninsula and eastern Brazil
ranges.Estrilda troglodytes: lowland to foothill grassy woodland, dense thickets, farmbush, swamp edge, and cultivation, from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward to southern Sudan, Eritrea, and western Ethiopia, and southward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and southwestern Kenya; some seasonal dispersal, introduced in Spain, western Persian Gulf coast, Singapore, Hawaii (island of Hawaii), and Lesser Antilles (Guadeloupe and Martinique)
ranges.Estrilda rhodopyga: lowland to foothill acacia savanna, grassland, and overgrown cultivation from northeastern Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia southward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, and Malawi
ranges.Paludipasser locustella: patchy in open upland short or burnt grassland of north-central to south-central Africa from Nigeria eastward to Tanzania, and in south from southern Angola eastward to central Mozambique
ranges.Ortygospiza atricollis: widespread but patchy in lowland to highland short dry grassland, marshy grassland, and treeless floodplains of sub-Saharan Africa, from southern Mauritania eastward to Cameroon, southward to northern Namibia, and from southern Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia southward through east Africa to southeastern Botswana southern Mozambique, and central and eastern South Africa, and westward in southern South Africa (west to Western Cape); nomadic in non-breeding season
ranges.Amadina erythrocephala: western Angola eastward to southern Zambia and southwestern Zimbabwe, and southward to southern South Africa
ranges.Amadina fasciata: lowland and foothill grassy and mopane woodland, and acacia or palm savanna, across the Sahel from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward to southern Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, southward through east Africa to southern Angola, and thence southward to southeastern Botswana and northeastern South Africa; nomadic and irruptive at times
ranges.Amandava formosa: locally in grassland and scrub of Peninsular India
ranges.Amandava subflava: widespread but patchy in sub-Saharan Africa (except rainforest and southwestern Africa), in lowland to montane grassland, open woodland, and marshes from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward to western Ethiopia, southward to Angola and northern Botswana, and from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda southward to eastern South Africa, nomadic during rains; also western Yemen (where possibly introduced?)
ranges.Amandava amandava: lowland to submontane grassland, marsh, damp grass, reeds, rice fields, tamarisk scrub, and villages, from Pakistan eastward to south-central China (including Hainan), and southward to Peninsular India, Thailand, and southern Vietnam, and from Java eastward through Lesser Sundas to Timor; introduced widely, including Iberia, north-central Italy, the Nile Valley (Egypt), central and eastern Arabian Peninsula, Malaysia, Singapore, Fiji (majin islands), Hawaii (most main islands), and Guadeloupe and Martinique (Lesser Antilles)
ranges.Granatina granatina: lowland to foothill acacia savanna, thornscrub, thickets in secondary woodland, and cultivation, from southern Angola eastward through southwestern Zambia to Zimbabwe, and southward to northern and northeastern South Africa and southern Mozambique
ranges.Granatina ianthinogaster: lowland to foothill semiarid thornbush, acacia thickets, and riparian woodland, from southeastern South Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia, and southward to central Tanzania
ranges.Uraeginthus angolensis: widespread south of Equator (except Congolian rainforest and southwest Africa), in acacia woodland, farmbush, and gardens from western Angola to northern Namibia, and from southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Tanzania, southward to southwestern Botswana, northern and eastern South Africa, and southern Mozambique; introduced in São Tomé
ranges.Uraeginthus cyanocephalus: lowland to foothill arid and semiarid savanna, acacia thickets, and thornscrub, from southeastern South Sudan, southern Ethiopia, and southern Somalia, southward to central Tanzania
ranges.Uraeginthus bengalus: lowland and foothill thornscrub, bushy grassland, and Sahel woodland from southern Mauritania and Senegambia eastward to southeastern Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and western Somali, southward to northeastern Angola, southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northern Zambia
ranges.Pyrenestes minor: foothill to submontane forest edge, secondary growth, rank streamside grass, reedbeds, and bracken briar, from southern Tanzania and Malawi southward to central Mozambique and adjacent eastern Zimbabwe
ranges.Pyrenestes ostrinus: lowland to foothill streamside gallery forest, forest edge, riparian scrub, and palm savanna, from eastern Ivory Coast and Ghana eastward to southern South Sudan, Uganda, and far western Kenya, and southward to northern Angola and northern Zambia
ranges.Pyrenestes sanguineus: lowland swamp-forest, tidal creek, brushy riparian along streams, and wet sedge in open forest, from Senegambia eastward to central Ivory Coast
ranges.Spermophaga poliogenys: lowland to foothill primary forest, old secondary forest, dense understory, and swamp-forest, from southeastern Cameroon and northern Republic of the Congo eastward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and adjacent western Uganda
ranges.Spermophaga ruficapilla: patchy in lowland to montane forest undergrowth, streams and thickets, from eastern Central African Republic and southern South Sudan southward through northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, to Burundi, and eastward to central Kenya and to the Usambara Mountains (northwestern Tanzania), and to southern Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Angola
ranges.Spermophaga haematina: lowland undergrowth in Upper Guinea rainforest, coastal palm forest, and thickets, from Senegambia eastward through southern Nigeria to western Central African Republic, and southward to Republic of the Congo, Cabinda (northeastern Angola), and to western, northeastern, and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Pytilia melba: patchy in lowland and foothill acacia thornscrub, thickets, and lightly-wooded savanna from southwest Mauritania and Senegal eastward to northeastern Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia, and southward (but avoiding Upper Guinea and Congolian rainforest), to western, eastern, and southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to Tanzania, thence southward to northern and eastern South Africa, and Lesotho and Eswatini
ranges.Pytilia lineata: lowland to foothill open woodland, wooded grassland, and brushy scrub, in western and central Ethiopia, old record from southeastern South Sudan
ranges.Pytilia afra: patchy in lowland to foothill open woodland, brushy scrub and thickets, tall grass savanna, and cultivation, from southern Republic of the Congo southward to Angola, and from Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Uganda southward to Botswana and northeastern South Africa; post-breeding nomadic wandering in arid habitats
ranges.Pytilia hypogrammica: lowland to foothill woodland, brushy grassland, farmbush, riparian forest, and coastal thickets, from western Guinea eastward to southern Chad and Central African Republic, and southward to coastal Ghana and Togo
ranges.Pytilia phoenicoptera: lowland dry woodland, thickets, and villages from Senegambia eastward through southern Mali, northern Cameroon, and Central Africa Republic, to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northern Uganda
ranges.Hypargos margaritatus: patchy in lowland dry woodland with dense thickets, sand forest, palm scrub, and dense thornscrub, in northeastern South Africa, Eswatini, and southern Mozambique
ranges.Hypargos niveoguttatus: patchy in lowland to foothill thickets, long grass, and riparian forest, from Rwanda and Burundi to central Kenya and southern Somalia southward to northeastern Angola, southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northern Mozambique, thence southward to northeastern Botswana, eastern Zimbabwe, and southern Mozambique
ranges.Euschistospiza dybowskii: disjunctly in lowland to foothill wooded grassland, thickets around granite hills, and weedy cultivation, from southeastern Senegal and southern Mali southward to Liberia and western Ivory Coast, and from central Nigeria eastward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southern South Sudan, and northwestern Uganda
ranges.Euschistospiza cinereovinacea: two disjunct ranges in miombo thickets and long grass in montane forest, in highlands of western Angola, and in the Albertine Rift from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, southwestern Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi
ranges.Clytospiza monteiri: patchy in lowland to foothill shrubby grassland, thickets, and fallow cultivation, from southeastern Nigeria and Cameroon eastward to southern South Sudan, Uganda, and far western Kenya, and southward to northern Angola and south-central Democratic Republic of the Congo
ranges.Lagonosticta senegala: widespread sub-Saharan Africa in lowland to montane savanna, grassland, and thornscrub, from Mauritania and Senegal eastward to central Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and western Somalia, southward locally to Angola and northern Namibia (but avoiding Congolian rainforest), and through east Africa, Zambia, and Mozambique to southern Botswana and central and eastern South Africa; introduced in Algeria
ranges.Lagonosticta nitidula: lowland to submontane reed and papyrus swamps, riverine thickets, riparian woodland and adjacent thornscrub,from northern Angola eastward to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Tanzania, and southward to northeastern Namibia, northern Botswana, and far northwestern Zimbabwe
ranges.Lagonosticta rufopicta: lowland acacia savanna, grassland, and marshes, from Senegambia eastward through northern Cameroon and Central African Republic to western Ethiopia, southward through South Sudan to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and western Kenya
ranges.Lagonosticta rara: lowland savanna, riparian areas, and farmbush, from southeast Senegal and Guinea eastward through Nigeria and Central African Republic to southern South Sudan, and southward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and adjacent northwestern Kenya
ranges.Lagonosticta larvata: lowland savanna across the Sahel from Senegambia eastward to northern Nigeria, Central African Republic, and southwest Sudan to western Ethiopia, southward through South Sudan to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Uganda
ranges.Lagonosticta rubricata: widespread but disjunct sub-Saharan range in lowland to montane grassland, bracken briar, and forest edge, from Senegal to Eritrea and eastern Ethiopia, southward to Gabon and Angola (avoiding Congolian rainforest and most of southwestern Africa), and through east Africa to southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mozambique, and thence southward to eastern and southern South Africa
ranges.Lagonosticta virata: patchy in lowland to foothill brushy grassland, acacia thickets, and rocky hillsides, in southeastern Senegal and southern Mali
ranges.Lagonosticta rhodopareia: lowland arid acacia scrub, riparian areas, and rocky hills, from western Ethiopia and southern South Sudan southward through northeastern Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, and southern Democratic Republic of the Congo to Angola, northeastern Namibia, and Mozambique, and southward to southeastern Botswana, northern and eastern South Africa, southward to KwaZulu-Natal), plus Lesotho and Eswatini (but absent in southwestern Africa)
ranges.Lagonosticta umbrinodorsalis: patchy in foothill brushy grassland, riparian scrub, and thickets near rocky hillsides and inselbergs, in northern Cameroon and southwestern Chad
ranges.Lagonosticta sanguinodorsalis: patchy in foothill arid bushy savanna, gallery forest, and thicket near rocky hillsides and inselbergs, in northern Nigeria and northwestern Cameroon
ranges.Prunella himalayana: mountains of central Asia to Afghanistan, southern Tibet, and northwestern India
ranges.Prunella collaris: patchy but widespread in Eurasia from lowland to alpine montane cliffs, rocky island sea-cliffs, scree, and alpine meadow above tree-line and up to snow-line, from southwestern Europe eastward through Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, and Tibet, to Ussuriland (Russia), North Korea, and Japan, and southward to Morocco, southern Iran, and Taiwan; local altitudinal migrant and wanderer to Spain, Levant, Arabian peninsula, and eastern China
ranges.Prunella immaculata: Nepal to southeastern Tibet and southwestern China; winters to northeastern Myanmar
ranges.Prunella rubeculoides: willow scrub, tussock grasses, and boggy areas in lake and stream edges in Himalayas from eastern Gilgit and Baltistan (northeastern Pakistan) eastward to Bhutan, and southwestern and southern and southeastern Xizang eastward to northeastern Qinghai, northern Gansu, and western Sichuan (central China)
ranges.Prunella atrogularis: disjunctly in montane to subalpine coniferous and deciduous forest, juniper scrub, and dense thorn-scrub, from Ural Mountains (northwestern Russia) and southwestern Siberia and western Mongolia southward to Kyrgyzstan and northwestern China, some populations migrate to northern Kazakhstan and southward to eastern Iran, northern Pakistan, northern India, and western Nepal
ranges.Prunella ocularis: breeds rocky slopes and pastures with scattered bushes and scrub in eastern Türkiye and the Caucasus southeastwards to northern Iraq and northern Iran and along the Zagros mountains to southern Iran, and disjunctly in the mountains of western Yemen; winters southward, some reaching Israel and northeastern Arabian Peninsula
ranges.Prunella modularis: lowland to montane scrub, tundra, woodland with dense understory, coniferous forest, and gardens, from British Isles and Scandinavia eastward to Ural Mountains (eastern Russia), and southward to Iberia, Balkans, Türkiye, and Caucasus; some populations migratory to northern Africa, Mediterranean Europe, Middle East, and western Iran; introduced to New Zealand (including Chatham Islands and all main subantarctic islands)
ranges.Prunella rubida: thickets, understory of pine, birch, and mixed-deciduous forest; also riverine scrub and thickets in winter, from southern Sakhalin and Kuril Islands (eastern Russia) southwards in mountains of Japan from Hokkaido to Shikoku in southern Japan; winters at lower elevations
ranges.Prunella montanella: foothill to montane boreal woodland, northern limits of coniferous and deciduous forest, dense willow or spruce taiga, and tree-line scrub, from western Siberia eastward through subarctic and boreal zones to northeastern Siberia, and southward to northern Mongolia; migrates to north-central and northeastern China, and Korean peninsula
ranges.Prunella strophiata: montane to alpine meadow, birch or oak woodland, pine forest, rhododendron scrub, and juniper or willow scrub, from eastern Afghanistan eastward through Himalayas to Tibet and central China, and southward to northern Myanmar; downslope dispersal in winter
ranges.Prunella koslowi: mountains of Mongolia and immediately adjacent northern China (Ningxia)
ranges.Prunella fulvescens: montane to alpine rocky slopes, and juniper scrub in high barren valleys, from eastern Kazakhstan and south-central Russia eastward to south-central Siberia and Mongolia, and southward to northeastern Afghanistan. northern India, and northern China, and disjunctly in Nepal and Tiber; some downslope dispersal in winter
ranges.Petronia petronia: southern Europe and north Africa eastward to northeastern China and south through Middle eastward to northern Afghanistan and central China
ranges.Montifringilla henrici: eastern Tibetan Plateau (northeastern Tibet and Qinghai)
ranges.Montifringilla adamsi: rocky steppe near streams and snowline in Ladakh (far northwestern India) and adjacent Tibet eastward to northeastern Qinghai and western Gansu, and southward to northern Nepal and northern Sikkim and adjacent Tibet; nomadic in winter but remains at high elevations
ranges.Montifringilla nivalis: southwestern and central Palearctic in rocky alpine barrens, meadows and buildings, from northern Spain eastward through Austria to southwestern and far south-central Russia, Xinjiang (northwestern China), and Mongolia, southward to Corsica and eastward through northern Afghanistan to southeastern Kazakhstan; mostly resident but some move to lower elevations and straggle elsewhere
ranges.Onychostruthus taczanowskii: Tibet to western China (Kokonor and Nan Shan Mountains to Sichuan)
ranges.Pyrgilauda ruficollis: stony and dry grass steppe and plateaus from southwestern Xinjiang eastward to Qinghai and western Gansu, in south from eastern Ladakh, northern Nepal, and northern Sikkim eastward to western Sichuan
ranges.Pyrgilauda davidiana: semi-desert and rocky steppe with short dry grass in the Altai mountains of south-central Russia, most of Mongolia eastward to Inner Mongolia (northeastern China), and in northeastern Qinghai (north-central China)
ranges.Pyrgilauda blanfordi: sandy, stony, and grassy plains from southeastern Xinjiang (southwestern China) and northern Ladakh, northwestern India eastward through northern Nepal and Sikkim and eastern Tibet to northern Sichuan (central China)
ranges.Carpospiza brachydactyla: arid Türkiye; winters to southwestern Arabia and northeastern Africa
ranges.Gymnoris xanthocollis: southeastern Türkiye to Iraq, southern Iran, eastern Afghanistan, Pakistan, and northwestern India
ranges.Gymnoris dentata: lowland to submontane arid savanna, open woodland, cultivation, and villages and towns, from southern Mauritania, Senegambia, and Guinea, eastward across Sahel to southern Sudan, Eritrea, and western Yemen, and southward to central Cameroon, South Sudan, and Ethiopia; nomadic wandering post-breeding
ranges.Gymnoris pyrgita: two disjunct populations in lowland and foothill arid savanna, acacia steppe, and open rocky woodland, from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward patchily in Sahel to central Sudan, and from Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia southward to southern South Sudan, northeastern Uganda, Kenya, and northern Tanzania
ranges.Gymnoris superciliaris: lowland to foothill savanna, open woodland, and riverine bush from southeastern Gabon and Republic of the Congo eastward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to northern Tanzania, southward through Angola, southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Malawi, to northern Namibia, northern Botswana, and Mozambique, thence southward through southern and eastern South Africa, Eswatini, and Lesotho
ranges.Passer griseus: lowland and foothill grassland, savanna, and villages from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward across the Sahel to central Sudan, eastern Eritrea, and eastern Ethiopia, and southward to northern Namibia, northern Botswana, northwestern Zimbabwe, and northern Mozambique, also Bioko (Gulf of Guinea); confusion with P. diffusus affects range limits in Tanzania
ranges.Passer swainsonii: lowland to montane arid highlands and plains, cultivation, and villages and towns, from Eritrea, Djibouti, Ethiopia, and adjacent Sudan and South Sudan, eastward to northern Somalia, and southward to northern Kenya
ranges.Passer gongonensis: lowland to foothill arid savanna, open brushy semi-desert, and thornscrub, from southeastern South Sudan, southern Ethiopia, and southern Somalia, and southward to Kenya, adjacent Uganda, and northern Tanzania
ranges.Passer suahelicus: foothill to submontane lightly-wooded grassland, open woodland, cultivation, parks, villages, and towns, from southern Kenya southward to central Tanzania, and patchily to southwestern Tanzania
ranges.Passer diffusus: lowland and foothill acacia and mopane woodland, clearings, and farmland, from western Angola eastward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to southern Tanzania, and southward to South Africa, but patchly in arid southwestern Africa; confusion with P. griseus affects range limits in eastern Africa
ranges.Passer melanurus: lowland lightly-wooded savanna, cultivation, and town throughout southern Africa from western Angola, northern Botswana, and southern Zimbabwe southward to South Africa, plus Lesotho and Eswatini
ranges.Passer eminibey: patchy in lowland to montane arid acacia savanna, especially near swamps or villages, from central Chad, southwestern Sudan, and Ethiopia southward to south-central Tanzania; nomadic wandering post-breeding
ranges.Passer motitensis: lowland dry rocky country and open acacia savanna from central Angola and Namibia eastward through Botswana and southwestern Zimbabwe to northern South Africa, plus northern Lesotho and northwestern Eswatini; nomadic in post-breeding season
ranges.Passer rufocinctus: foothill to montane acacia savanna, open woodland, cultivation, and towns, in Rift Valley highlands from central Kenya southward to northern Tanzania
ranges.Passer shelleyi: foothill grassy savanna with sparse trees, brushy semi-desert, open woodland, and cultivation, from southeastern South Sudan eastward to eastern Ethiopia and adjacent Somalia, and southward to Uganda and far western Kenya
ranges.Passer cordofanicus: lowland to foothill arid savanna, semi-desert, cultivation, and villages, in eastern Chad and southwestern Sudan
ranges.Passer cinnamomeus: Himalayas of northeastern Afghanistan to northeastern Asia, Korean Peninsula, and Sakhalin, and southward through hills south of Brahmaputra and northern southeastern Asia; northeastern populations migrate southward
ranges.Passer montanus: Eurasia, southeastern Asia, Malayan Peninsula, Indonesian Archipelago, and Philippines
ranges.Passer ammodendri: river valleys in sandy and stony desert and semi-desert with saxaul and other bushes and trees, from western Uzbekistan, northern Turkmenistan, southern and eastern Kazakhstan, and northern Xinjiang eastward through southern Mongolia, and northern Gansu, western Inner Mongolia, and northern Ningxia (north-central China)
ranges.Passer zarudnyi: desert of south-central Asia (Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan)
ranges.Passer simplex: desert with scattered trees and bushes, including wadis and oases in the Sahara from central Tunisia, northern Morocco, Algeria, and Libya southward patchily to southern Mauritania, central Mali, southern Niger, Chad, and central Sudan
ranges.Passer moabiticus: riverine and lakeside scrub and semidesert in southern Türkiye, northern Syria, and Cyprus southward to the Dead Sea basin and the Gulf of Aqaba, Jordan, and to Mesopotamia, also in the Seistan region of easternmost Iran, western Afghanistan, and possibly adjacent northern Baluchistan (western Pakistan)
ranges.Passer luteus: lowland to foothill arid sandy savanna with few trees from southern Mauritania and northern Senegal eastward across Sahel to eastern Sudan, Eritrea, and northeastern Ethiopia; widely nomadic post-breeding, reaching Western Sahara, Cabo Verde, and Canary Islands
ranges.Passer euchlorus: southwestern Arabian Peninsula (southwestern Saudi Arabia and western Yemen; Djibouti and northwestern Somalia)
ranges.Passer flaveolus: northern Myanmar to Thailand, Malayan Peninsula, and southern Vietnam
ranges.Passer insularis: Socotra and associated islets Samha and Darsa
ranges.Passer hispaniolensis: lowland to submontane open shrubbery, cultivation, arid steppe, semi-desert, and urban areas, from Iberia, Sardina, and Greece eastward through Caucasus to southern Kazakhstan and northwestern China, and southward to northern Africa, Levant, and Afghanistan; some populations migrate southward to Sahara, Nile Valley (Egypt), Arabian Peninsula, and western India; introduced to Madeira, Canary Islands, and Cabo Verde
ranges.Passer pyrrhonotus: far southeastern Iran to Pakistan and northwestern India
ranges.Passer castanopterus: lowland dry acacia savanna, rocky areas, coastal cliffs, and towns, from Ethiopia, Djibouti, and Somalia southward to northern and eastern Kenya
ranges.Passer italiae: Italian Peninsula, Corsica, Sicily, and Crete
ranges.Passer domesticus: native range extends from British Isles and Scandinavia to northern Africa, eastward through southeastern Siberia and western southeastern Asia; introduced around human population centers almost globally elsewhere (except most of Asia)
ranges.Dendronanthus indicus: breeds Russian Far East to southeastern China (and formerly southern Japan); winters to southern and southeastern Asia
ranges.Motacilla flaviventris: open country and streams throughout Madagascar
ranges.Motacilla bocagii: locally in forest of southern São Tomé
ranges.Motacilla capensis: lowland to montane grassland, wetlands, and towns from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Uganda eastward to central Kenya, thence southward to Burundi and northwestern Tanzania, and western Angola eastward to Zambia, and southward through Namibia and Zimbabwe to South Africa and southern Mozambique
ranges.Motacilla clara: patchy in sub-Saharan Africa, along lowland to montane rocky rivers and streams in forest, from Guinea to southeastern Nigeria southward to Angola, plus Bioko (Gulf of Guinea), and Eritrea and Ethiopia southward to southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and southwestern Tanzania, and through Zimbabwe and southern and eastern South Africa
ranges.Motacilla cinerea: lowland to montane fast-flowing streams in forest, foothill rivers, and flatland canals with artificial waterfalls, from British Isles and Scandinavia eastward to Siberia and Kamchatka, and southward to Azores, Madeira, and Canary Islands, southern Europe, Caucasus, northeastern China and Japan, and from Afghanistan eastward through Himalayas to northeastern India; migrates southward to northern and eastern Africa, southern and southeastern Asia, Philippines, Greater Sundas, and Indonesia
ranges.Motacilla flava: lowland to montane marsh, wet meadows, grassy tundra, bogs, damp steppe, and waterside pastures, from British Isles and Scandinavia eastward to northwestern Siberia, and southward to northwestern Africa, Mediterranean Europe, Nile Valley (Egypt), Arabian Peninsula, northern Afghanistan, and western China; migrates southward to sub-Saharan Africa and Indian subcontinent
ranges.Motacilla citreola: breeds north-central Europe to north-central Siberia and northeastern China, and southward in Himalayas; winters to central Asia, Indian subcontinent, southeastern Asia, and southeastern China
ranges.Motacilla tschutschensis: lowland to foothill grassy swamps, wet meadows, grassy tundra, and grassy clearings in forest, from northern Siberia eastward to northern and western Alaska, and southward to northern Mongolia, northeastern China, and Commander and Kurile Islands; migrates southward to southeastern Asia, Philippines, Greater Sundas, Indonesia, and northern Australia
ranges.Motacilla aguimp: widespread sub-Saharan Africa in lowland to montane wetlands, rivers, parks, and towns (but mostly absent from Congolian rainforest except along large rivers, eastern Somalia, and the Namib and Kalahari deserts), from Senegambia eastward to Sudan (and northward along the Nile to southern Egypt), southward to southern Africa
ranges.Motacilla maderaspatensis: Himalayas (northern Pakistan to Bangladesh) and Peninsular India
ranges.Motacilla alba: widespread in lowland to montane open habitats, including seashore, river edge, farmland, short grassland, and towns, from Iceland, British Isles, and Scandinavia eastward to Siberia and western Alaska, and southward to northwestern Africa, Europe, Levant, northern Iran, northern India, southern China, and Japan; northern populations migrate to African Sahel, eastern Africa, southern and southeastern Asia, and northern Philippines
ranges.Motacilla grandis: breeds Japan from Hokkaido southward to Kyushu; winters to China, Korean Peninsula, and Taiwan
ranges.Motacilla samveasnae: lower Mekong delta of Cambodia and Laos
ranges.Tmetothylacus tenellus: foothill to submontane flat or undulating grassland, favoring lush grassland with tussocks, in Drakensburg of eastern South Africa and adjacent Lesotho; some downslope dispersal in austral winter
ranges.Hemimacronyx chloris: patchy and local in submontane to montane open short grassland, often with tussocks, in highlands of western and central Kenya
ranges.Macronyx sharpei: patchy and local in submontane to montane open short grassland, often with tussocks, in highlands of western and central Kenya
ranges.Macronyx capensis: lowland to montane shortgrass grassland and rocky Fynbos from northern Zimbabwe and nearby Mozambique southward through southeastern Botswana and eastern South Africa, Lesotho, and Eswatini, to coastal south and southwestern South Africa
ranges.Macronyx croceus: lowland to montane dry grassland, open cultivation, arid scrubby grassland, and open clearings in miombo woodland, from Senegambia and southern Mali eastward to southern Sudan, South Sudan, and western and southeastern Kenya, and southward (in the west) to northwestern Angola, and southward (in the east) through eastern Zamibia and Zimbabwe to eastern South Africa
ranges.Macronyx fuelleborni: highland grassland, dambo, and miombo from northern Angola through central Democratic Republic of the Congo to southern Tanzania southward to southern Angola and Zambia
ranges.Macronyx flavicollis: foothill to montane open grassland on highland plateaus in central Ethiopia
ranges.Macronyx aurantiigula: lowland to foothill arid grassland with acacia and bush, coastal grassland, plateau grassland, and open dry woodland, from southern Somalia southward through southeastern Kenya to northeastern Tanzania; some seasonal dispersal with rains
ranges.Macronyx ameliae: disjunctly in lowland to montane grassland from western and central Kenya to northern Tanzania, and from eastern Angola, southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and southern Tanzania southward to northern Botswana, Malawi, northwestern Mozambique, and eastern Zimbabwe, and from coastal southern Mozambique to northeastern South Africa
ranges.Macronyx grimwoodi: patchy in foothill moist short grassland on plains and in river valleys in southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, northeastern and central Angola, and northwestern Zambia
ranges.Anthus sylvanus: Himalayas (eastern Afghanistan to Nepal and southeastern China)
ranges.Anthus godlewskii: southern Siberia to Mongolia, China, Tibet, and northeastern India

ranges.Anthus campestris: breeds central and southern Europe and northwestern Africa (Morocco eastward to Tunisia) eastward to northwestern and south-central Mongolia, northwestern Kazakhstan, northern Afghanistan, and far northwestern China, also locally in Middle East; winters in sub-Saharan Africa (mainly in the Sahel), Arabian Peninsula, and southwestern Asia

ranges.Anthus similis: mountains of southwestern Mali, Guinea, and Sierra Leone to western Himalayas, southwestern India, and central Myanmar
ranges.Anthus vaalensis: lowland grassland and overgrazed or burnt clearings from western Angola eastward through southern Democratic Republic of the Congo to southern Tanzania, southward through Zambia and Malawi to Namibia, Botswana, and eastern South Africa and adjacent Mozambique (but not southern Namibia and western South Africa); some post-breeding dispersal
ranges.Anthus nyassae: lowland and foothill broadleaf woodland, wooded savanna, and miombo from southeastern Gabon and southern Republic of the Congo, eastward through southern Democratic Republic of the Congo to southern Tanzania, and southward to northern Namibia, northern Botswana, Malawi, Zimbabwe, and nearby Mozambique

ranges.Anthus pallidiventris: lowland grassland and forest clearings from southern Cameroon to northwest Angola and eastward through Gabon, southern Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo; locally nomadic in non-breeding season
ranges.Anthus melindae: coastal lowland grassland and dunes from southern Somali to coastal southeastern Tanzania
ranges.Anthus leucophrys: widespread sub-Saharan Africa in lowland and foothill lightly-wooded savanna, brushy grassland, and floodplains from southern Mauritania and Senegambia to southeastern Sudan, Eritrea, and Somalia southward to South Africa

ranges.Anthus crenatus: foothill to montane steep rocky scree slopes, alpine grassland with boulders or shrub, and grassy Karoo, in South Africa and Lesotho

ranges.Anthus brachyurus: disjunctly in short open grassland, mostly foothill to montane, from southeastern Gabon to northeastern Angola eastward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Uganda, thence southward through northwestern Zambia and central Mozambique to eastern South Africa and southern Mozambique; may be erratic or nomadic

ranges.Anthus spragueii: breeds prairies and plains of North America; winters to southern Mexico
ranges.Anthus chii: disjunctly in varied grasslands including open fields with short grass, in western and central Panama, from the llanos of central Colombia eastward to the Guianas, almost throughout Brazil (except western Amazonas and western Acre) westward to far southeastern Peru (Madre de Dios), and southward to east-central Argentina (La Pampa)

ranges.Anthus chacoensis: locally in Chaco of eastern Paraguay and northern Argentina

ranges.Anthus nattereri: locally in southeastern Brazil, southeastern Paraguay, and northeastern Argentina
ranges.Anthus correndera: dry puna grassland, bogs and wetland edges, and Patagonian steppe from the Andes of central Peru (Ancash), locally in southeastern Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil (Santa Catarina), southward to far southern Chile and Argentina and the Falkland Islands
ranges.Anthus gustavi: lowland tundra scrub and swampy taiga from northern Russia eastward to eastern Siberia, Kamchatka, and Commander Islands, and southward to northeastern China and adjacent Ussuriland; migrates to Philippines, Borneo, and Wallacea
ranges.Anthus nilghiriensis: montane grassland of southwestern India (western Tamil Nadu and Kerala)
ranges.Anthus trivialis: lowland to montane open woodland, woodland edge, and grassland with scrub or scattered trees, from Britain and Scandinavia eastward to central Siberia, and southward to southern Europe, Caucasus, northern Pakistan through Kashmir; winters to sub-Saharan Africa and southern India
ranges.Anthus hodgsoni: lowland to montane taiga edge, rocky ground in open forest, scrub above treeline, and scrub with isolated trees, from northwestern Russia eastward to Kamchatka and northern Japan (Hokkaido), and southward through central China to Himalayas from Kashmir eastward to south-central China; migrates to southern India, southeastern China (including Hainan), and Taiwan, and to southeastern Asia, Borneo, and Philippines

ranges.Anthus roseatus: breeds eastern Afghanistan to southeastern Tibet and southwestern China; winters to southeastern Asia

ranges.Anthus rubescens: breeds northern Alaska including Aleutians through northeastern Canada and western Greenland, and southward through mountains of western North America to Arizona and New Mexico; winters to south-central Mexico and Florida
ranges.Anthus pratensis: breeds Iceland and Faroe Islands through western and northern Europe eastward to western Russia; winters to northern Africa and central Asia

ranges.Anthus spinoletta: patchy in lowland to montane alpine meadows, short grassland, and rocky scree with thickets, from mountains of central and southern Europe eastward to eastern Kazakhstan and Mongolia, and southward to Caucasus, northern Iran, and northwestern and central China; most migrate to western Europe, northwestern Africa, Middle East, Pakistan, and southern China

ranges.Callacanthis burtoni: Himalayas from northwestern Pakistan eastward to Nepal and rarely Sikkim
ranges.Procarduelis nipalensis: montane to alpine oak and fir forest, rhododendron scrub, bamboo, alpine meadow, and rocks above tree-line, from Kashmir eastward through Himalayas to Tibet and central China, and southward to northern Myanmar and south-central China
ranges.Leucosticte nemoricola: alpine meadows and subalpine scrub from eastern Kazakhstan northeastward to Altay and Tuva regions (south-central Russia), western and northwestern Xinjiang (northwestern China), and western Mongolia; in south through northeastern Afghanistan, eastward in Karakorum, Tibet, and Inner Himalayas to far northern Myanmar and northwestern Yunnan, northern Qinghai, Gansu, and southern Shaanxi (north-central China); winters to lower elevations

ranges.Leucosticte australis: mountains of southeastern Wyoming, Colorado, and north-central New Mexico
ranges.Haemorhous mexicanus: desert scrub, cacti, and grassland, and varied woodland and anthropogenic habitats from southern British Columbia eastward to Nova Scotia (southwestern to southeastern Canada) southward in western USA through Mexico to northern Oaxaca and Veracruz, including Baja California and Isla Guadalupe; introduced to Hawaii, and to northeastern USA from whence has spread to southeastern Canada to Florida
ranges.Haemorhous cassinii: mountains of southwestern Canada to central Mexico and southern Baja California
ranges.Haemorhous purpureus: breeds in moist coniferous and mixed forests and riparian woodland from southern Yukon and southern Northwest Territories eastward to Newfoundland (southwestern to eastern Canada) southward in western USA to southern California, and in eastern USA from northern Minnesota eastward to Maine, and southward in the Appalachians to West Virginia; winters southward to northern Baja California (northwestern Mexico) and throughout eastern USA sporadically to northern Florida
ranges.Rhodospiza obsoleta: locally in mountains of southeastern Türkiye to northern China and northern Pakistan
ranges.Rhynchostruthus louisae: local in lowland to foothill thornscrub slopes, rocky outcrops, and dry wadis with giant euphorbia, in northern Somalia
ranges.Chloris chloris: woods, gardens, and oases from British Isles and northern Scandinavia eastward to northwestern Kazakhstan, northern Xinjiang (northwestern China), and Krasnoyarsk (south-central Russia); in south to Iberian Peninsula, Madeira, and Canary Islands, Morocco to Tunisia (northwestern to north-central Africa), northeastern Egypt, and Mediterranean to Türkiye, Cyprus, Levant, northern Iraq, and northern Iran through Altai region to southeastern Kazakhstan; some withdrawal from north in winter
ranges.Chloris sinica: lowland to submontane broadleaf and conifer woodland, secondary growth, orchards, parks, and gardens, from northeastern China eastward to Kamchatka, and southward through Japan southward to Ogasawara (Bonin) Islands, Korean Peninsula, and eastern China to Vietnam; northernmost populations migrate to Japan and southeastern China
ranges.Chloris spinoides: foothill to montane oak and conifer forest, rhododendron thickets, scrub above tree-line, and gardens, from northern Pakistan eastward through Himalayas to northeastern India and adjacent China, and southward to western Myanmar; some downslope dispersal in winter, occasional nomadic incursions
ranges.Chloris ambigua: montane open coniferous and deciduous forest and woodland, alpine meadows, and scrub in southern China (southern Sichuan and southeastern Tibet), northeastern Arunachal Pradesh, and northern Myanmar southward to northwestern Vietnam, northern Laos, and northern Thailand
ranges.Linurgus olivaceus: disjunctly in montane cloudforest, from southeastern Nigeria, western Cameroon, and Bioko (Gulf of Guinea) in west Africa, and from southern South Sudan, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo to Burundi, eastward to eastern Uganda and central Kenya, and southward through eastern Tanzania to Malawi in east Africa; some downslope movement in non-breeding season
ranges.Crithagra leucopygia: lowland to foothill lightly wooded savanna and acacia thornscrub across the Sahel from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward through southern Algeria to Sudan and Eritrea, thence southward to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and northwestern Uganda
ranges.Crithagra mozambica: sub-Saharan Africa from southern Mauritania and Senegal eastward to Eritrea and Ethiopia, southward (but avoiding rainforest) from Cameroon, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and western Kenya, to Angola, northeastern Namibia, northern Botswana, Zambia, and Mozambique (avoiding Namib and Kalahari deserts), and thence southward through Zimbabwe to eastern South Africa, widely nomadic in non-breeding season; introduced in São Tomé (Gulf of Guinea), Mafia Island (Tanzania), Mascarenes, Hawaiian Islands (mainly Oahu and Hawaii), and Puerto Rico
ranges.Crithagra citrinelloides: wet montane grassland and forest edges disjunctly from Eritrea and Ethiopia to western Kenya
ranges.Crithagra frontalis: foothill to montane grassland, forest clearings, secondary forest, marsh, bracken-briar, cultivation, and gardens, from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo eastward to Uganda and southwestern Kenya, and southward to western Tanzania and northeastern Zambia
ranges.Crithagra hyposticta: foothill and montane forest, bracken-brier, and eucalypt plantations disjunctly from southern South Sudan and (reported) central Ethiopia, and from northwest Uganda and western Kenya southward through southern Kenya and eastern and southern Tanzania, Malawi, adjacent Zambia, and northern Mozambique
ranges.Crithagra capistrata: lowland and foothill primary and secondary forest, marsh, and brushy grassland from Gabon and Republic of the Congo eastward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to easternmost Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Burundi, southward to western Angola, southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and northern Zambia
ranges.Crithagra koliensis: patchy in foothill papyrus swamp from Uganda and southwestern Kenya southward to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and northwestern Tanzania
ranges.Crithagra scotops: lowland to montane scrub, wooded patches in highveld grassland, and gardens from southwestern South Africa (Western Cape) through southern South Africa (to KwaZulu-Natal), eastern Lesotho, and northern Eswatini, to northeastern South Africa (Limpopo); partly nomadic
ranges.Crithagra rothschildi: lowland to montane shrubby plateaus, dry rocky highland, juniper woodland, scrub, and edge of cultivation, in western Saudi Arabia and Yemen
ranges.Crithagra atrogularis: patchy in lowland savanna, acacia thornscrub, grassland near water, and miombo from southeastern Gabon eastward (avoiding Congolian rainforest) to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and southeastern Kenya, southward through Angola, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, to Namibia, Botswana, and western and central South Africa, eastward to northeastern South Africa and Lesotho
ranges.Crithagra reichenowi: lowland to submontane arid bushy scrub, thornscrub, open woodland, and cultivation edges, from Ethiopia, southeastern South Sudan, and Somalia southward to eastern and southern Tanzania
ranges.Crithagra xanthopygia: lowland to montane open woodland and scrub in Eritrea and central Ethiopia, and possibly Djibouti
ranges.Crithagra citrinipectus: patchy in lowland to foothill palm savanna, dry miombo and mopane woodland, scrub, and semiarid grassland, from southern Malawi, eastern Zimbabwe, and Mozambique southward to southeastern South Africa; nomadic post-breeding
ranges.Crithagra dorsostriata: lowland to montane grassland, lightly wooded savanna, and thornscrub from southeastern South Sudan, central Ethiopia, and Somalia, southward through Uganda and Kenya to central Tanzania; dry-season nomad
ranges.Crithagra flavigula: patchy in foothill and submontane semiarid desert, steep rocky scrub, acacia thornbush, and tussock grassland, in central Ethiopia
ranges.Crithagra xantholaema: lowland to submontane semiarid desert, acacia thornscrub, limestone gorges with scrub, and juniper woodland, in central and southern Ethiopia
ranges.Crithagra donaldsoni: lowland to foothill arid savanna, acacia thornscrub, and semi-desert scrub, from east-central Ethiopia and Somalia southward to central Kenya; nomadic post-breeding
ranges.Crithagra buchanani: lowland to foothill dry thornscrub, acacia savanna, scrub, and grazed grassland, in southern Kenya and northeastern Tanzania
ranges.Crithagra sulphurata: patchily distributed in lowland to montane woodland, grassland, thornscrub, and Protea bush from northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and central Kenya southward to central Angola, Zambia and Mozambique, and then southward to eastern and southern South Africa (westward to Western Cape); erratic dry-season wandering
